title: Explaining Autonomous Decisions in Swarms of Human-on-the-Loop Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
venue: arXiv cs.HC
evidence: Videos V3-V5 showed "two sUAS reporting simultaneously" in a four-sUAS human-on-the-loop interface, with freeze-frame SA questions; participants "were not able to interact directly with the prototype" (Experimental Design; Limitations and Future Work).
method: Video-based between-groups study of minimal versus detailed explanation boxes in a human-on-the-loop interface for an sUAS swarm; SAGAT-style freeze-frame probes and raw NASA-TLX.
evaluation: 78 crowd workers (one of five 90-second videos each) plus 7 domain experts; SA of both events 64% minimal vs 48% detailed; correct mission perception 23% vs 62.5%; TLX medians 66-86.
contribution: Evidence that minimal event-action explanations preserve operator situation awareness better than detailed ones in human-on-the-loop sUAS swarms, and that operators readily accept incorrect autonomous perceptions.
flag: agents per person: 4 sUAS in the interface, with 2 reporting simultaneously in videos V3-V5; human measure: SAGAT-style freeze-frame situation awareness (64% both events understood with minimal explanations vs 48% with detailed, a 16-point contrast), automation-bias correctness (23% when the sUAS perception was wrong vs 62.5% when right) and raw NASA-TLX medians (66 to 86). Check the evaluation floor: percentages and between-group contrasts only, with no significance tests, effect sizes or confidence intervals, and about 15-16 crowd workers per video. Participants watched pre-recorded 90-second videos and could not interact with the prototype, so no takeover was performed and the configure, suspend and acknowledge controls are untested design features; the 'Needs Human Control' failure scenario was only an expressed intention to take over. Participant counts do not reconcile (109 recruited, 78 analysed, stated exclusions sum to 34).

title: Leveraging Augmented Reality for Improved Situational Awareness During UAV-Driven Search and Rescue Missions
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: The field study used "a pre-configured Parrot ANAFI Quadcopter UAV" (Sec. VI-A) and "In future, we aim to scale VizCom-AR to support multi-UAV missions" (Sec. VII).
method: VizCom-AR, a HoloLens 2 augmented-reality system that visualises UAV-derived geolocations and points of interest for on-site operators, replacing radio voice exchange during search-and-rescue response.
evaluation: 16 students in 8 two-person teams, VizCom-AR vs radio, two landmark conditions; completion time median 88 s vs 164 s; NASA-TLX mental demand 46 vs 63; geolocation error 1.3-2.9 m.
contribution: An augmented-reality channel for sharing UAV-derived geolocations between remote and on-site responders, roughly halving point-of-interest localisation time against radio communication in a field study.
flag: agents per person: 1 UAV; human measure: task completion time (median 88 s with AR vs 164 s with radio in the unknown-landmark condition) and raw NASA-TLX (mental demand 46 vs 63, frustration 24 vs 60, effort 36 vs 59). The human side is measured and contrasted against a radio baseline, so condition (1) is met, but the setting is single-UAV and multi-UAV support is explicitly future work, hence exclude-E4 under the 2026-11-14 ruling; the two humans (remote operator and on-site operator) are a human-human team, not several automated agents. Also worth noting if the maintainer reconsiders: no p-values or statistical tests anywhere, situation awareness reported only as 5-point Likert figures in Figs. 13-14 with no numbers in the text, OSO distance travelled reported only qualitatively, and the sole timing figure is a 5-second database polling interval.

title: OSU-Wing PIC Phase I Evaluation: Baseline Workload and Situation Awareness Results
venue: arXiv cs.HC
evidence: "The PICs were expected to pause the system operations based on the adverse Weather update" (Sec. 3.2) while responsible for 25 to 100 concurrently active UAS across 10 or 24 nests (Sec. 2.1).
method: Human-factors evaluation of one pilot-in-command supervising a Wing delivery UAS fleet across nest-count and PIC-ratio conditions; workload estimated from wearable sensors, SA from in situ probes.
evaluation: 6 PICs, three conditions (10:Low, 24:Low, 24:High); mean active UAS 27.33, 30.67, 76.33; overall workload 28.51, 29.39, 29.21 (never above 60); SA probe accuracy 92.59%, 92.59%, 96.30%.
contribution: Baseline evidence that one pilot can supervise roughly 76 concurrently active delivery UAS with workload inside the normal range and above 92% situation-awareness probe accuracy, contradicting earlier fleet-size limits.
flag: agents per person: 25 to 100 active UAS over 10 or 24 nests (observed means 27.33, 30.67, 76.33), one pilot in an operations-centre console, so condition (2) holds under the control-room ruling; human measure: sensor-estimated overall workload (28.51 to 29.39 on 0-100, never into overload) and in situ SA probe accuracy (above 92% in every trial, 96.30% in 24:High). Check the sample: 7 recruited, 6 analysed, and session 1 split three PICs per condition, so the nest contrast rests on n=3 per cell; the SA percentages carry no statistical test at all. Several reported F values look implausible for this design (DAA:Double workload F(531,2124)=1.63, p<.001, eta2=.05), and Table 17 gives 1,031 total interactions for 24:Low against 1,034 in Sec. 3.4.1. This is a technical report rather than a peer-reviewed paper. PICs paused fleet operations but never took manual control of an individual UAS, and no system latency is reported.

title: A Study on Human-Swarm Interaction: A Framework for Assessing Situation Awareness and Task Performance
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: "20 robots executed PSO in an open environment" (Sec. IV-A) while operators guided the swarm and marked hazardous cells unknown to it, with SAGAT and SART taken during each 5-minute task.
method: Framework plus tablet interface for human-swarm interaction; operators guide a 20-robot PSO swarm in a target search, marking hazard cells; objective (SAGAT) and subjective (SART) SA measured.
evaluation: 31 participants, within-subjects, six 5-minute tasks over three hazard types and two attempts; centroid active robot distance 7.8 m to 2.5 m for Dis (significant); SAGAT vs performance rho -0.61.
contribution: A human-swarm interaction framework pairing objective and subjective situation-awareness measures with a centroid-based performance metric, validated in a 31-participant tablet study guiding a 20-robot search swarm.
flag: agents per person: 20 simulated robots; human measure: SAGAT objective SA, SART subjective SA and centroid active robot distance to target. Check the evaluation floor: there is no baseline interface or control condition, only attempt (A1 vs A2) and hazard-type contrasts, tested with Wilcoxon and Spearman (objective SA vs performance -0.61, objective vs subjective SA -0.51, subjective SA vs performance not significant); exact p-values are given only for the Spr contrast (p=0.14). Performance improved for the Dis hazard (7.8 m to 2.5 m) but worsened for Mov (2.4 m to 9.5 m), so the conclusion that task performance increased in attempt 2 is overstated. Simulation only (CoppeliaSim plus Android tablet), no latency figures, and the operator can push or mark but not halt or veto a robot action.

title: HRI-SA: A Multimodal Dataset for Online Assessment of Human Situational Awareness during Remote Human-Robot Teaming
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: "In the cave, two robots explored in parallel, but only one robot's camera feeds were shown" and the operator "had to monitor and occasionally override robots' decisions at intersections by issuing way-points" (Sec. III-A, III-C).
method: Multimodal dataset (eye movements, pupil, biosignals, interactions, robot data) from 30 operators in simulated search-and-rescue; random forest and MLP models detect perceptual situation-awareness latency online.
evaluation: 30 participants, tunnel (1 robot) and cave (2 robots); 1155 PSAL vs 6071 no-PSAL points; leave-one-group-out F1 80.38% eye plus context vs 67.63% eye-only and 71.65% context-only; AUC 0.97.
contribution: First public multimodal dataset for online detection of operator situation-awareness gaps during remote multi-robot search-and-rescue teaming, with baseline classifiers reaching 80% F1 from gaze plus context.
flag: agents per person: 1 in the tunnel run and 2 in the cave run; human measure: perceptual situation-awareness latency (1155 PSAL points, 30 s threshold) plus gaze and pupil features. Check whether a half-single-robot design is acceptable: in the cave only one robot's camera feeds were shown, so part of the multi-agent load is nominal, though the executive panel let the operator select, stop and task both robots. No statistical test backs the claim that combining feature sets significantly improved performance. Subjective questionnaire and biosignal data are released but not analysed, and the paper reports no tunnel vs cave SA-latency contrast. Table I repeats identical values for the KNN and MLP eye-tracking rows (possible transcription error). runtime_interceptor yes rests on the operator stopping or overriding robots at intersections, not on the SA detector itself.

title: NuHF Claw: A Risk Constrained Cognitive Agent Framework for Human Centered Procedure Support in Digital Nuclear Control Rooms
venue: arXiv cs.AI
evidence: The governance safety gate 'intercepts autonomous execution' and requires human approval once estimated risk exceeds thresholds (Sec. risk-constrained agent runtime); the case study recruited three graduate students for about 3 hours of cursor and click logs on a two-reactor control-room simulator, but the reported workload scores (1RO 55.83, 2RO 33.33, 3RO 36.67) are ACT-R model output, and no NASA-TLX values, human error probabilities, SA scores or performance figures are reported.
method: Risk-constrained cognitive agent runtime for digital nuclear control rooms: LSTM event perception, ACT-R cognitive twin estimating workload and situation awareness, Bayesian-network human error probability, and a governance safety gate requiring human approval.
evaluation: Single case study on the HTR-PM600 full-scope simulator shutdown procedure; 3 students' cursor logs (Sec. 4.4 says six); modelled workload table and explained variance above 0.9; no baseline, no ablation, KRAIL under 150 s.
contribution: Cognitive-risk agent runtime for digital nuclear control rooms that couples modelled operator workload and error probability with a governance gate escalating high-risk autonomous actions to human approval.
flag: agents per person: the control room covers 2 reactors with three operator roles, which counts under the 2026-11-14 control-room ruling, but the case study follows one shutdown sequence and the number of units the agent monitors at runtime is never stated. human measure: NONE usable. Workload is ACT-R model output, the paper says post-experiment NASA-TLX corroborated it but reports no TLX values, and there are no human error probability, SA or task-performance figures and no baseline or ablation, so it fails the evaluation floor (participants but no reported human figures). Check: the 3 vs 6 participant inconsistency between the case-study section and Sec. 4.4; the Bayesian network structure, thresholds and risk values are not reported either.

title: HELP: Human-Efficient Large-Scale Robot Post-Training with Rollout Segmentation
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: Two specialized operators supervise twelve robots concurrently, a Teleoperator giving remote interventions and recovery demonstrations and a Floor Operator who monitors the fleet, triggers takeovers and performs resets (Abstract and Sec. pipeline); takeover is forced from a Bluetooth keyboard or flagged by a 2B Qwen-VL takeover predictor, and on takeover the client discards stale actions, but nothing about the humans is measured.
method: Human-efficient large-scale VLA post-training pipeline: role-split human supervision of 12 concurrent robots with predictive and manual takeover plus resets, and VLAC-CUT automatic rollout segmentation for data curation.
evaluation: 4 lab manipulation tasks vs base policy and vs HITL-only at matched human budget; success 20-55 percent to 80-95 percent, throughput 1.7x-4.2x, gain amplification mean 2.15x throughput and 2.21x success; VLAC-CUT MAE 7.56 vs 12.35; episodes 30-105 s.
contribution: Post-training pipeline in which two role-specialised operators supervise twelve robots concurrently with predictive takeover and automatic rollout segmentation, amplifying policy success and throughput gains per unit of human labour.
flag: agents per person: 6 on average (2 operators for 12 concurrent robots; the paper never splits the load per role). human measure: NONE. 'Human efficiency' is defined as policy performance gain and throughput per unit of human labour and time, which is a system metric, and I read both halves of the paper: there are no takeover counts, takeover times, intervention rates, operator workload or error figures, and no user study. Check: the fleet-takeover setting is exactly the right level for Pillar 5 and the gate fails only on condition (1), so the maintainer may want it kept as mechanism evidence under (a); the predictive takeover model's own accuracy is never evaluated, and Appendix B mentions packet loss and missing control slots without quantifying them.

title: MRPilot: Supervising and Intervening LLM-Based Multi-Robot Teams through Mixed Reality
venue: arXiv cs.HC
evidence: Sec 5.3: each participant supervised a team of three separately controlled heterogeneous robots (fixed-base arm, wheeled delivery robot, drone) through linked situated and overview views; Sec 4.2.4: "Stop pauses execution and allows a new intervention"; measured human outcomes incl. SART overall SA Mdn 7.00 chat vs 33.50 MRPilot (W=3, p<.001) and NASA-TLX mental demand 75.25 vs 23.00 (t(19)=-10.28, p<.001).
method: Mixed reality supervision interface for LLM-planned multi-robot teams: ambiguity resolution, pre-execution plan review, live monitoring, and robot-level or team-level repair via stop, delete, revert, play.
evaluation: Within-subjects VR two-story home, 20 participants, MRPilot vs voice-and-text LLM chat with identical planner; intervention completion times, prompt counts, NASA-TLX, SART, MDMT, TOROS, perceived control; Quest 3; no latency reported.
contribution: Shows that a mixed reality supervision layer over an LLM-driven three-robot team lowers operator workload and raises situation awareness, trust, transparency and perceived control against a chat baseline across eight intervention types.
flag: agents per person: 3 separately controlled robots supervised as one team from linked situated plus overview views, so the control-room ruling is satisfied and the participant supervises rather than is affected by the automation; human measure: NASA-TLX (mental demand 75.25 vs 23.00, dz=-2.30; effort 75.50 vs 16.25; frustration 72.75 vs 13.5, all p<.001), SART overall SA Mdn 7.00 vs 33.50 (p<.001), MDMT capacity trust 2.94 vs 6.75 (p<.001), TOROS explainability 3.07 vs 6.36 (p<.001), perceived control Mdn 3.67 vs 6.50 (p<.01), plus 7 of 8 intervention-type completion times faster (e.g. failure recovery Mdn 356.87 s vs 201.79 s, p=.036; authorization not significant, p=.206). Check: plan review plus Stop is arguably criterion (a) as a human approval gate, but the paper reports no safety-rate metric at all (no collision, violation, hazard or false-halt rate), so (a) was not credited and runtime_interceptor is human-mediated only; the 9 intervention events per task were predefined scripted branches, VR simulation only with no physical robots, and Sec 7.3 concedes communication latency was not captured; no halt or end-to-end latency figure anywhere and the backend is a cloud GPT-5.4 API, so no edge-deployment cell; SART overall SA is a composite index not a percentage; Sec 6.1 reports Authorization-Access with medians but SD values, an internal inconsistency; abstract claims of higher transparency and trust are all borne out in Sec 6.2.

title: Design and Evaluation of a Collaborative Teleoperation Interface for Multi-Operator Multi-Robot Systems in Challenging Environments
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: A comparative user study with 16 participants compared co-located operators with a shared interface, remote operators with a shared interface, and co-located operators with individual interfaces (Abstract and Sec. Study Design); each operator drove 1 robot (HUSKY A300 with UR10, or DJI Phantom 3) while the shared visualisation showed both, so a crew of 2 covered 2 separately controlled robots; freeze-probe SA accuracy 91.1 vs 80.0 vs 69.3 percent and NASA-TLX 38.2 vs 57.7 vs 42.0.
method: Shared-visualisation collaborative teleoperation interface for multi-operator multi-robot teams, compared within subjects against individual per-robot interfaces in a Unity nuclear power plant digital twin disaster-response task.
evaluation: 16 participants (8 pairs), 3 conditions; SA freeze probe 91.1/80.0/69.3 percent (F=39.23 p<.001), NASA-TLX 38.2/57.7/42.0 (F=48.77 p<.001), collisions 0.9/3.0/3.3, handoff latency 6.6/11.8/17.3 s, GSR 6.5/8.2/6.9 uS; no latency figures.
contribution: Shared-visualisation interface for multi-operator multi-robot teleoperation that cuts completion time, collisions and handoff latency and raises freeze-probe situation awareness relative to per-robot individual interfaces.
flag: agents per person: 2 (each operator directly controls 1 robot but monitors both through the shared view; a 2-person crew covering 2 separately controlled robots, which satisfies condition (2) under the 2026-11-14 control-room ruling). human measure: freeze-probe SA 91.1 vs 69.3 percent, NASA-TLX 38.2 vs 57.7, collisions 0.9 vs 3.3, plus GSR and HR. Check: this is manual teleoperation, not automation deferring to a person, so criterion (e) holds only through operator-to-operator handoff, and handoff latency is never defined; collisions are a side metric not a safety-mechanism claim; no means are reported for heart rate, HRV, blink rate, trust subscales, facial temperature or the communication subcounts; skill covariate r=-.81 for collisions comes from only 8 pairs.

title: Human Situational Awareness and Workload during Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicle Hazard Monitoring: A Cross-Platform Study
venue: arXiv cs.HC
evidence: Each trial involved one platform type, a ground vehicle or an aerial drone, and the two were never monitored together (Sec. III Experimental Design): 1 autonomous ego platform per participant, with 8 ground or 14 aerial surrounding vehicles acting as hazards rather than supervised automation; SART overall SA 25.45 (visual-haptic) vs 21.28 (visual-only) on ground and 21.52 vs 15.98 aerial, NASA-TLX 4.64-4.81 ground vs 5.44-5.79 aerial.
method: Within-subject AirSim study of supervisory hazard monitoring; three interface modalities (visual-only, haptic-only, visual-haptic) crossed with ground vs aerial autonomous platform; bHaptics TactSuit X40 directional cues.
evaluation: 18 participants, 6 conditions, 18 trials each; SART and NASA-TLX against a visual-only baseline; SA modality F=9.35 p<.001 etap2=.355, scenario F=6.96 p=.017; workload scenario F=25.24 p<.001; no latency reported.
contribution: Cross-platform within-subject study showing haptic and visual-haptic cues raise operator situation awareness over visual-only during supervisory hazard monitoring, and that aerial monitoring costs more SA and workload than ground.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one autonomous ego platform per trial; the 8 ground and 14 aerial surrounding vehicles are hazards, not separately supervised automation). human measure: SART overall SA and NASA-TLX weighted workload, with full repeated-measures ANOVA and Hedges g figures. Check: single-agent supervision, so exclude-E4 under the 2026-11-14 ruling even though the human measurement is the strongest in this batch; the person is also closer to a monitor than a controller and never takes over (button presses recorded but not reported); text and Table II disagree on ground visual-haptic SA (23.69 vs 25.45); the paper itself says platform effects are confounded with hazard count (8 vs 14) and haptic mapping.

title: Level of robot autonomy and information aids in human-robot interaction affect human mental workload – an investigation in virtual reality
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "Each of 20 participants performed his/her own task while interacting with two virtual robots in a manufacturing environment" (Abstract); at low LORA the robots "adapted the request for interaction to idle times between individual operator tasks" (Sect 2.3, Variables)
method: VR mixed-reality manufacturing simulation; 2 (level of robot autonomy, between) x 2 (multi-modal information aid, within) design with one operator performing a grammatical-reasoning task while two industrial robots hand off quality-control checks
evaluation: 20 participants, 2 robots each; NASA-TLX null (IA off 57.45 vs on 55.48, F(1,16)=1.15, p=.300; LORA p=.573); HRT errors fewer at low LORA (p=.025, eta2=.28), HRT errors+misses p=.005 eta2=.39; HT response time p=.004 eta2=.42 and LORA x IA p=.002 eta2=.47
contribution: VR study showing that two robots deferring their interaction requests to operator idle times, plus audio-visual pre-handoff signalling, improves operator task performance although perceived workload does not change
flag: agents per person: 2 (two virtual industrial robots); human measure: NASA-TLX plus HT/HRT error, missed-trial and response-time rates. Check that NASA-TLX showed NO effect, so the workload claim rests entirely on performance measures and a compensatory-control argument; no SA measure at all; VR simulation, n=20 with LORA between subjects (10 per cell); the robots hand a decision to the human rather than the human taking over control

title: A Novel Metric of Continuous Situational Awareness Monitoring (CSAM) for Multi-telepresence Coordination System
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "Participants are asked to monitor either one or multiple robots as they navigate through a simulated environment" (Abstract); "During the multi-robot sessions the screen split into four panels" (Sect 4, Materials and Methods)
method: Within-subject comparison of a 2D monitor versus a VR headset for passive supervision of one versus four autonomously navigating simulated TurtleBot3 robots in Gazebo; proposes CSAM, a continuous report-disparity measure of situation awareness
evaluation: 10 CS students, four 5-min sessions; mean report disparity single-monitor -2, single-VR -0.5, multi-monitor -1.8, multi-VR 0.6; VR mean absolute error 0.55 vs monitor 1.9 objects; post-trial 7-point ratings workload 4.6 VR vs 3.7 monitor, immersion 4.8 vs 4.5, comfort 4.1 vs 6.2, resolution 3.9 vs 6
contribution: VR head-mounted presentation keeps a remote operator closer to accurate object counts than a 2D monitor when passively supervising a fleet of four autonomous robots, at the cost of higher workload and lower confidence
flag: agents per person: 4 robots in the multi-robot condition (1 in the control condition); human measure: CSAM report disparity plus 7-point immersion, workload and comfort ratings. No inferential statistics anywhere, n=10 computer-science students, all four conditions run in one fixed order with no counterbalancing, and the operator role is purely passive observation with no takeover or control, so criterion (e) rests on situation awareness alone

title: Exploring the Concept of Goal-Oriented Human-Machine Interface Design in an Agricultural Use Case
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
evidence: "The experimental design confronted the participants with an unfamiliar user interface concept in a new work context that involved simultaneously monitoring two highly automated machines, asking them to identify and solve two performance threats" (Sect 6, Results)
method: Task-based usability test of a goal-oriented performance-indicator HMI for monitoring and controlling highly automated combine harvesters; simulated cab screen plus tablets showing a conventional UI and the new UI for a second remote machine
evaluation: 15 operators, 2 machines, two 3-min incident scenarios; perceived overview of the second machine M=3.53 (critical drop) vs M=4.00 (minor drop) on a 5-point scale, felt able to make adjustments 3.13 vs 3.60; UEQ+ KPI 1.42 (SD 1.05) against a published 0.38 benchmark; trust in automation correlates with experience r(13)=.54, p=.038
contribution: Expert-user evaluation of a goal-oriented hierarchical performance-indicator interface for supervising two highly automated harvesters, reporting perceived situation awareness, usability and trust across a critical and a minor incident
flag: agents per person: 2 machines (one in-cab, one remote); human measure: self-reported situation awareness and functional-sufficiency statements, UEQ+ scales, trust in automation. WEAKEST RECORD OF THIS BATCH and the one most likely to be overturned to exclude-E2: descriptive means and SDs only, no baseline interface, no inferential test of the interface itself, and the only interface comparison is to a UEQ+ score from a different published study (Schrank et al., 0.38). The critical-drop vs minor-drop contrast is the only internal condition contrast and is untested

title: Optimizing Human Operations of Multiple Semi-autonomous UAVs: Impacts of Video Gaming Experience and UAV Quantities
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
evidence: "The number of UAVs was a within-subjects variable, which varied across three levels: 2, 4, and 6" (Sect 2.3, Design); "reaction time referred to the duration from when the UAV issued an alert to when the participant confirmed the target and marked it on the map" (Sect 3.1)
method: 2 (video-gaming experience, between) x 3 (number of semi-autonomous UAVs: 2, 4, 6, within) Unity simulation of a search-and-rescue task in which each UAV auto-searches and alerts the operator, who confirms or dismisses targets
evaluation: 18 participants; two-way mixed ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc; alert reaction time 20.28s with 2 UAVs vs 47.31s with 6 (F(2,32)=15.81, p<.001, p=.01 pairwise); NASA-TLX 49.77 vs 61.54 (p=.02); SART 6.57 vs 4.49 (p=.01); accurate targets F(2,32)=30.86, p<.001; completion time 335.67s high-gaming vs 442.44s low (p<.001)
contribution: Controlled simulation identifying four semi-autonomous UAVs as the span-of-control plateau for a single operator, with alert reaction time, target accuracy, NASA-TLX and SART all degrading at six UAVs
flag: agents per person: 2, 4 or 6 semi-autonomous UAVs; human measure: reaction time to a UAV target alert, target-marking accuracy, NASA-TLX, SART. Strongest record of the batch. One error to check: Sect 3.1 states accurate targets "with 6 UAVs (M = 13.90, SD = 1.42)" which contradicts Table 1 (4.67 and 6.11) and the sentence's own claim that 6 was lower than 2 and 4, so it appears to be a typo. Gaming experience was self-categorised by questionnaire, not randomised; simulation only, n=18 (9 per gaming group)

title: An XR-Based Simulation Platform for Human–Automation Collaboration in Industrial Work Machines
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
evidence: "A single operator supervised three semi-autonomous wheel loaders, manually performing manipulation-intensive tasks such as bucket loading, while autonomous agents handled transport, dumping, and return phases" (Abstract), but "The objective of the study was not to perform a comprehensive evaluation of operator performance or human-automation collaboration efficiency" (Sect 4)
method: XR human-in-the-loop platform (Mevea physics simulation, motion seat, haptic steering and joysticks) with a task-level state machine, pure-pursuit path following and proportional bucket control; control authority transfers between operator and autonomous controller per phase
evaluation: 6 participants, 3 wheel loaders, four 7-min sessions (two single-machine manual, two sequential three-machine); only machine-side figures reported - fuel-consumption curve by phase, cumulative material collected, Gantt chart of machine states; no human measure quantified, only the qualitative remark that awareness of non-active machines became more demanding
contribution: An XR, physics-based human-in-the-loop platform for system-level experimentation on sequential supervision of several semi-autonomous work machines, demonstrated with one operator and three wheel loaders
flag: agents per person: 3 wheel loaders; human measure: NONE quantified - the paper reports only fuel use, material collected and state timelines, and states explicitly that it is a platform demonstration rather than an evaluation of operator performance. Satisfies the multi-agent gate and the handoff topic but fails the evaluation floor, hence exclude-E2 rather than E4. Worth re-screening if the group publishes the structured study they promise

title: Supporting multi-objective decision making within a supervisory control environment
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "results on the SA probe showed increases in the error distance for map object placement ... as a function of increases in block difficulty level" and "participants had significantly fewer fixations within the relevant display region, the map, one and two minutes prior to the SA probe during the high level of task load" (Sect 2, Previous Research Within SCOUT) - stated without figures
method: Overview of the SCOUT multi-UAV supervisory control testbed, a summary of previously published eye-tracking, pupillometry, HRV and SA-freeze-probe findings, plus a proposed route-optimality metric and a risk-threshold (perceived value) reweighting of expected utility for decision support
evaluation: 20 volunteers, 3 UAVs each, easy/medium/hard task-load blocks (tasking every 75/45/15s) with SA freeze probes, SmartEye eye tracking and Zephyr HRV; all human effects described as significant but with no numeric values; the only numbers given are machine-side plan scores (optimal 1565 clustered vs 1635 dispersed, top-10 SD 57 vs 127)
contribution: Summary of the SCOUT three-UAV supervisory control testbed and its eye-tracking and heart-rate correlates of workload and situation awareness, with proposed route-optimality and risk-bias metrics for future decision aids
flag: agents per person: 3 UAVs; human measure: SA freeze-probe placement error, pupil diameter, HRV and chat-task error - every one of them reported without figures and cited to refs 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9. The paper says of itself "This paper reviewed previous research conducted within SCOUT" (Sect 4), so exclude-E3 is also arguable. The maintainer may prefer to screen the cited primary sources (Coyne and Sibley 2015; Jasper et al. 2016) instead

title: Human-agent teaming for effective multirobot management: Effects of agent transparency
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "we discuss the implications of patterns of interaction between software-based intelligent agents (IA) and humans, and give examples of experiments that verify their usefulness" (Sect 1); results given only as "trust calibration (correct rejections and correct positive responses-hits) improved for the latter two conditions compared with the L1 (baseline information) condition" (Sect 4)
method: Two design patterns for human-agent teaming in multirobot supervision - a single RoboLeader supervisory agent mediating several autonomous vehicles, and the IMPACT pattern with separate asset-manager, plan-manager and mission-monitor agents - organised by the Situation awareness-based Agent Transparency (SAT) model
evaluation: Narrative summary of two prior simulation experiments varying SAT level (L1 vs L1+2 vs L1+2+3; then L1+2 vs L1+2+3 vs L1+2+3+U) with three heterogeneous vehicles, plus a convoy study with a 66%-reliable advisory agent; no participant counts, no statistics and no effect sizes reported in this paper
contribution: Design-pattern overview arguing that agent-transparency information at the action, reasoning and predicted-outcome levels calibrates operator trust when one person supervises several autonomous vehicles through one or more intermediary agents
flag: agents per person: 3 heterogeneous vehicles plus 1 to 3 intelligent agents; human measure: trust calibration (correct rejections and hits), subjective trust and decision performance - all described qualitatively with no figures, cited to Mercado et al. 2016 (Human Factors 58(3) 401-415) and Stowers et al. 2016. Design-pattern overview chapter, so exclude-E3 is also arguable. Recommend the maintainer screen Mercado et al. 2016 directly, since that is the primary study behind these claims

title: Designing a support system to mitigate pilot error while minimizing out-of-the-loop-effects
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science (including subseries Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence and Lecture Notes in Bioinformatics)
evidence: "This article describes a design pattern for human-autonomy teaming in which a human operator is supported by two cognitive agents" (Abstract); "in 42 % of the cases the assistant system had to escalate to the final level of overriding the pilot to avoid damage" (Sect 4.2, Results)
method: Dual-mode cognitive automation: a subordinate delegate agent executing task-based commands plus an assistant system that models the pilot's information processing with a Colored Petri net, schedules interventions with EUROPA against the predicted time of damage, and escalates warning, highlighting, relief and finally command override
evaluation: 17 German Armed Forces officers and cadets, ABA design (assistant off, on, off) over three simulated reconnaissance missions; performance-loss penalty score significantly lower with the assistant active, while SAGAT situation awareness, NASA-TLX workload and reconnaissance task score showed no significant difference; 31 interventions logged, 42% escalated to override, 36% resolved after the first two steps
contribution: An assistant system that schedules its interventions against the time remaining before damage and escalates from warning to override only when the pilot's modelled reaction sequence would not finish in time, cutting performance loss without measurable cost to situation awareness or workload
flag: agents per person: 2 cognitive agents (delegate agent plus assistant system) but only 1 unmanned aircraft - THE DECISION MOST LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED in this batch, since the maintainer may read this as a single-vehicle ground control station and rule exclude-E4; I included it because the pattern is explicitly a human teaming with two distinct automated agents, one of which can override the other at runtime. Human measure: penalty-based performance loss (significant), SAGAT SA and NASA-TLX (both null). Figures are shown only as box plots with significance asserted in prose; no test statistics or p-values appear in this paper and the numbers are in the German-language ref 14 (Theissing, Liegel and Schulte 2015), which the maintainer should obtain

title: Factors affecting performance of human-automation teams
venue: Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing
evidence: Chapter 27 (pp. 331-340, Baker and Keebler), Introduction: "this paper will review several factors that affect the performance of H-A systems"; the abstract calls it a "high-level review". title: Evaluation of early ground control station configurations for interacting with a uas traffic management (UTM) system
venue: Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing
evidence: "A flight crew operated an integrated ground control station if a single individual occupied both the client operator and ground control station roles" (Sect 4); "The GCSOs coordinated with the PIC ... they generated the flight plans and monitored the aircraft from their GCS display during the operations" (Sect 3)
method: Post hoc human-factors comparison of integrated versus non-integrated ground control station display and role configurations during NASA UTM Technical Capability Level 2 field tests, using post-run 7-point ratings, observation and end-of-day focus groups
evaluation: 11 flight crews, 69 runs over 9 days, up to 5 concurrent flights across 5 GCS locations but one aircraft per crew; 7-point ratings integrated vs non-integrated: situation awareness 5.1 (SD 2.1) vs 3.9 (SD 2.0), workload 3.9 (SD 0.7) vs 3.6 (SD 1.5), communication quality 6.7 vs 6.6, procedure integration 6.2 vs 5.4; no statistics, authors call the analysis informal and exploratory with substantial missing data
contribution: Exploratory field-test comparison showing that integrating the UTM client with the ground control station display, and the two roles in one person, raised reported situation awareness without changing workload or communication
flag: agents per person: 1 aircraft per flight crew (up to 5 concurrent operations, but each flown by a separate crew in its own operational volume under one UTM service); human measure: 7-point situation awareness and workload ratings, SA 5.1 vs 3.9 favouring integrated displays. CLOSEST CALL FOR INCLUSION: if the maintainer applies the ruling that one person watching many entities under a single central automation counts, and treats the UTM service as that automation, this becomes includable - but no individual operator here supervised more than one aircraft, and the paper itself defers fleet operators to future work ("it may also be useful ... to evaluate the role of operators who will control large fleets", Sect 7). It is also weak on the floor: no statistics, inconsistent and missing ratings

title: A human-autonomy teaming approach for a flight-following task
venue: Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing
evidence: "At the start of a scenario, the operators had up to 30 aircraft to flight-follow after takeoff until landing" (Sect 2.3); "This version of the ground station was designed to monitor, with the help of automation, a large number of aircraft (up to 30)" (Sect 2.2)
method: Within-subject HAT versus No-HAT comparison of a flight-following ground station built around the Autonomous Constrained Flight Planner recommender, with play-based electronic checklists, display of the recommender's factors and weights, operator reweighting and voice interaction
evaluation: 6 participants (4 dispatchers, 2 pilots), up to 30 aircraft each, two counterbalanced 50-min scenarios with about six diversions per scenario, paired-samples t-tests; confidence that own diversions were appropriate 7.83 (SD 1.47) HAT vs 6.33 (SD 2.07) No HAT, t(5)=4.39, p=.01; HAT preferred for situation awareness M=8.67 and for reducing workload M=8.33 on a 1-9 scale; reliance on the recommender not different (p=.41); acceptability of recommendations p=.12
contribution: Part-task study showing that making a diversion recommender's factors, weights and task allocation visible and negotiable raises an operator's confidence in diversion decisions while flight-following up to thirty aircraft
flag: agents per person: up to 30 aircraft under one ground-station automation, plus the ACFP recommender and play automation; human measure: subjective preference ratings for situation awareness and workload, and confidence in own diversion choice, of which only confidence reached significance (t(5)=4.39, p=.01). n=6 and every reported measure is subjective - the behavioural data is explicitly reported elsewhere (ref 16), so the maintainer may want that companion paper screened and may judge the subjective-only evidence too thin for the floor

title: Information displays and crew configurations for UTM operations
venue: Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing
evidence: Sect. 3.2: participants reported their workload as medium (m = 4.16 out of 7), with integrated crews feeling more loaded (m = 4.8) than distributed crews (m = 3.8); at Test-Site 1 one USS Op submitted and managed the flight volumes for four flight crews.
method: Field observation, end-of-day questionnaires and 18 group interviews across 23 UAS flight crews at six NASA UTM TCL2 test sites; integrated versus distributed crew configuration compared.
evaluation: 23 crews, 149 end-of-day and 19 shakedown survey responses; self-reported workload 4.8 vs 3.8 of 7, vigilance 5.8 vs 5.3, easy information finding 2 of 3 vs 40 percent; no inferential statistics.
contribution: Field study of UTM flight crews showing that collocating the airspace-services operator with a crew raises workload and vigilance, while distributing one operator across four crews shifts information acquisition to voice.

title: Understanding Human Situation Awareness in One-to-Many Human-Robot Interaction Scenarios
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
evidence: Sect. 4.2 Results: only TargetInfo showed a statistically significant reduction in objective SA when degraded (p = 0.000); Sect. 3.1 the interface serves a single-target search task involving 20 robots controlled by particle swarm optimization.
method: Tablet interface for one operator guiding a 20-robot PSO swarm through a simulated spreading-fire task; seven interface versions degrading six information dimensions; within-subject.
evaluation: 40 participants, 20 robots, 5-min tasks per condition; SAGAT median SA 41.9 degraded vs 59.5 full information for TargetInfo (Wilcoxon p = 0.00); SAGAT and SA Level 2 correlate -0.62 to -0.65 with nearest-robot performance.
contribution: Degrading swarm-interface information narrows a single operator's attention to one robot, and only target and position information produces a measurable loss of objective situation awareness.
flag: agents per person: 20 robots; human measure: SAGAT objective situation awareness plus SART subjective SA and robot-proximity task performance; cleanest record in this batch, both gate conditions plainly met; chapter located inside the AI 2025 LNAI 16371 volume at pp. 479-490.

title: Investigating Human-Robot Teams for Learning-Based Semi-autonomous Control in Urban Search and Rescue Environments
venue: Journal of Intelligent and Robotic Systems: Theory and Applications
evidence: Sect. 5.2: both interaction effort and task performance were significantly better for the semi-autonomous mode compared to the teleoperation mode, F(1, 160) = 506.2, p < 0.001.
method: MAXQ hierarchical reinforcement-learning semi-autonomous controller for USAR robot teams; one operator controls 5, 10, 15 or 20 robots in semi-autonomous and teleoperation modes in USARSim.
evaluation: 21 participants, 8 trials each; interaction effort and task performance F(1,160) = 506.2 p < 0.001; exploration-time slope 6.7 s per robot semi-autonomous vs 73.2 s per robot teleoperation; Likert stress 1.9 vs 3.1, experience 4.1 vs 3.1.
contribution: A learning-based semi-autonomous controller lets one operator run rescue-robot teams of up to 20 robots with far lower interaction effort and self-reported stress than teleoperation.
flag: agents per person: 5, 10, 15 and 20 rescue robots; human measure: operator interaction effort (share of exploration time spent controlling robots), composite task performance and 5-point Likert stress and experience ratings; the paper reports two samples - 21 participants in the main operator-to-robot-ratio study and 13 in the separate 1-robot and 4-robot learning comparison - so do not read the 13 as the main N.

title: Planning and Monitoring Multi-Job Type Swarm Search and Service Missions
venue: Journal of Intelligent and Robotic Systems: Theory and Applications
evidence: Sect. 5.2: the Hybrid Model aid enabled participants in the experimental group to determine the performance of the swarm and identify anomalies more accurately than their counterparts in the control group, and the results were statistically significant.
method: Between-groups user study of a Hybrid Model prediction aid for planning swarm size and monitoring multi-job-type swarm search-and-service missions with vehicles breaking off to service jobs.
evaluation: 24 participants split experimental vs control, 5 planning and 5 monitoring trials; swarm size F(1) = 5.70 p = 0.026, cost F(1) = 10.03 p = 0.004, decision time F(1) = 26.46 p = 0.000; NASA-TLX mental 53.75 vs 66.67, temporal 18.33 vs 30.42.
contribution: A predictive Hybrid Model aid helps operators size and monitor a service swarm with lower workload and better anomaly discrimination, at the cost of longer decision times.
flag: agents per person: one swarm of vehicles whose size the participant chose (tens of vehicles) plus the jobs it serviced; human measure: NASA-TLX across six subscales, anomaly-detection correctness and decision time; the performance-decision ANOVA was NOT significant (F = 1.993, p = 0.172), so the accuracy claim rests on the descriptive tally in Fig. 8 while only decision time, swarm size and cost reached significance.

title: Modeling and Predicting Trust Dynamics in Human–Robot Teaming: A Bayesian Inference Approach
venue: International Journal of Social Robotics
evidence: Sect. 5: we tested the proposed method using an existing dataset involving 39 human participants interacting with four drones in a simulated surveillance mission, obtaining a root mean square error of 0.072 against 0.101 for ARMAV and 0.139 for Optimo.
method: Beta-distribution model of temporal trust learned per participant by Bayesian inference from the history of robot performance; clustering of fitted parameters identifies three trust-dynamics types.
evaluation: Existing human dataset, 39 participants each supervising four drones; trust-prediction RMSE 0.072 vs ARMAV 0.101 and Optimo 0.139, t(39) = 5.7 p < .001 Cohen's d = 0.91; RMSE stable across report gaps q = 2 to 25.
contribution: A Beta-distribution Bayesian model predicts an individual's moment-to-moment trust in a four-drone team more accurately than ARMAV or Optimo and separates three distinct trust-dynamics types.
flag: agents per person: 4 drones; human measure: repeated self-reported trust ratings taken from an existing human-subject dataset; no new human experiment is run here and the only contrast is model-fit accuracy against two prior models rather than an experimental condition on the person, so the maintainer may well read this as a model paper and overturn to exclude-E2 - it survives only under the clause allowing a dataset of people's behaviour.

title: Human–Swarm Interaction Simulation Platform to Assess Sense of Agency
venue: Journal of Control, Automation and Electrical Systems
evidence: Sect. 4: the full operator control mode presented a reaction time average of 5.5s and a resolution time average of 11.4s; the partial operator control mode presented a reaction time average of 0.7s and resolution time average of 9.8s.
method: Human-swarm simulation platform with four levels of automation over conflict detection, robot selection and takeover; two levels-of-automation cases assess the operator's sense of agency during swarm supervision.
evaluation: 4 volunteers, 12 runs per level-of-automation case; takeover reaction time 5.5 s full operator control vs 0.7 s partial, resolution time 11.4 s vs 9.8 s; single-item sense-of-control 6 vs 5 on a 7-point scale; no inferential statistics.
contribution: A human-swarm simulation platform shows that automating conflict detection and robot selection cuts operator takeover reaction time roughly eightfold while lowering the reported sense of control.
flag: agents per person: an urban autonomous robot swarm sharing a path with pedestrians (several robots, one flagged for takeover at a time); human measure: takeover reaction time, conflict resolution time and a one-item sense-of-control rating; only 4 volunteers, no statistics, and the paper frames itself as a platform and proof of concept, so this is the record most likely to be overturned to exclude-E2 on the evaluation floor.

title: Exploring remote operation of heavy vehicles—findings from a simulator study
venue: Human-Intelligent Systems Integration
evidence: Section 6: 'The present study explored the requirements for remote operator work in supervisory control of ten heavy vehicles in hub-to-hub transportation by means of a simulator study'; s5.2.1 'The remote assessment task was characterised by keeping track of the ten vehicles ... and responding to alarms by transitioning to remote assistance or remote driving'.
method: Exploratory simulator study of a remote operator workstation for ten automated trucks on a public road and in a hub; three defined tasks (assessment, assistance, remote driving) with five scripted events; think-aloud, observation, post-interviews and NASA-TLX.
evaluation: 15 participants, 1.5 h session, 10 trucks each: NASA-TLX reported only as a boxplot per scenario with no medians or test statistics given; 'A Friedman test was performed but it did not show any statistically significant differences'; only demographics are numeric (mean age 38.4, SD 9.03).
contribution: Simulator exploration of remote operator work supervising ten automated heavy vehicles, documenting situation-awareness, out-of-the-loop, trust and attention-management challenges and finding task transitions easier than expected.
flag: agents per person: 10 (ten trucks in parallel, so condition 2 is comfortably met) human measure: NASA-TLX plus think-aloud and interviews. Excluded on the evaluation floor only: no quantitative human figure is reported anywhere in the results - the TLX appears solely as Figure 7 boxplots described in words ('slightly higher medians') and the one inferential test is a null Friedman with no statistic or p value. If the maintainer is willing to read medians off Figure 7, or counts the null Friedman across five scenario conditions as a condition contrast, this flips to include, and it is the record in this batch most likely to be overturned. Otherwise it is qualitative-plus-boxplot evidence and E2 stands.

title: A communication paradigm for human-robot interaction during robot failure scenarios
venue: Human-Machine Shared Contexts
evidence: Sect. 14.5 Results: the number of participants who understood a robot needed to be reset was significantly higher (P = .04 using McNemar's test) during runs when the app was present (12 of 20) compared to the default (5 of 20).
method: Smartphone app providing push and pull failure communication from a group of robot vacuums; 2x4 mixed-groups factorial dual-task study with a concurrent balloon game blocking line of sight.
evaluation: 20 participants supervising 3 active robots (5 present, 2 deliberately broken) plus a secondary game; reset understanding 12 of 20 vs 5 of 20 P = .04; robot cleaning time F(1,16) = 17.052 P < .001; confidence 4.65 vs 3.70 P = .005; TLX mental demand P = .055.
contribution: Push and pull smartphone failure communication from a group of robots more than doubles the share of out-of-the-loop supervisors who correctly diagnose which robot needs help.
flag: agents per person: 3 active robots out of 5 in the pen; human measure: correct identification of the help each robot needed, confidence in understanding robot behaviour, time and attention allocation and NASA-TLX; WARNING - this is a book chapter in Human-Machine Shared Contexts and protocol v1.5 lists book chapters as exclude-E3 even when they report an original experiment, so the maintainer must settle that conflict before the include stands.

title: Managing delay-induced challenges in remote monitoring of uncrewed space habitats: The impact of forecasting telemetry visualizations
venue: Acta Astronautica
evidence: Sect. 4 Results: participants in Group D reported the highest temporal demand, 55.63 (22.03), significantly higher than the Delay plus Forecast group at 32.08 (23.30), one-way ANOVA p = .020.
method: Between-groups experiment with a MATLAB habitat simulator and an Open MCT ground-control interface; three conditions - no delay, 207 s one-way delay, and delay plus a physics-based forecast cone.
evaluation: 35 participants monitoring one habitat with battery, interior temperature zones and pocket-door loops; temporal demand 37.95 control, 55.63 delay, 32.08 delay plus forecast (p = .020); composite performance pairwise C vs D+F p = 0.0279; post-hoc power only for large effects.
contribution: Forecast cones over delayed telemetry let ground operators of an uncrewed deep-space habitat hold system stability with significantly lower temporal demand than delay alone.
flag: RULING: maintainer ruling 2026-11-14: one habitat with several loops is single-agent, not a control room over many processes | was include | agents per person: one simulated habitat supervised through three concurrent loops (battery charge, interior temperature zones, pocket door) under a single central habitat automation; human measure: NASA-TLX temporal demand plus a composite temperature and battery stability score; MULTI-AGENT IS THE WEAK POINT - this is one habitat, not a fleet, and it passes only under the maintainer's many-loops-of-one-plant-automation clause, so exclude-E4 is a live alternative; the paper states that SA itself was not directly measured, and only temporal demand reached significance.

title: Effects of platooning on signal-detection performance, workload, and stress: A driving simulator study
venue: Applied Ergonomics
evidence: Sect. 3.1: in the Detection Task condition participants attained a high mean detection rate (94.7%) and a low mean false alarm rate (0.8%); Sect. 2.3 participants were automatically transported within a five-car platoon, with the third car being the ego car and all cars fully automated.
method: Driving-simulator experiment, three 40-min runs inside a five-car fully automated platoon under No Task, Voluntary Task and Detection Task instructions, counterbalanced within-subject.
evaluation: 22 participants, five-car platoon; hit rate 94.7 percent and false alarms 0.8 percent; DSSQ engagement loss in all conditions, TLX elevated for Detection Task, heart rate drop dz = 0.96 p < 0.001, PERCLOS F(2,42) = 7.09 p = 0.002.
contribution: Drivers in a fully automated five-car platoon sustained near-ceiling threat detection over 40 min, with an imposed monitoring task raising workload and stress rather than degrading vigilance.
flag: agents per person: 5 platooned vehicles moving synchronously under one automation; human measure: signal-detection hit and false-alarm rate, NASA-TLX, DSSQ stress states, heart rate, SDNN, LF to HF ratio and PERCLOS; the participant could only ever have taken over the ego car and no automation malfunction was actually staged, so this qualifies as multi-agent only through the maintainer's explicit platoon clause and is a reasonable exclude-E4 candidate.

title: Does automation trust evolve from a leap of faith? An analysis using a reprogrammed pasteurizer simulation task
venue: Applied Ergonomics
evidence: Sect. 1.1.3: the pasteurization system had two subsystems, the pump subsystem and the heating subsystem; the pump system was set by default to be manual, however participants had the option to toggle between automatic and manual, while operators were required to operate the heating subsystem manually.
method: Two replications of Muir and Moray (1996); operators ran a reprogrammed single pasteurizer plant under nine pump control-error and display-error conditions, rating nine trust constructs after each run.
evaluation: Experiment 1 n = 10, Experiment 2 n = 12 engineering majors, 9 conditions, 80 iterations per run; stepwise and Bayesian regression - dependability was the best initial trust predictor (B10 = 1.50x10^3) against faith (B10 = 79.57); performance scores 79.13 to 90.17.
contribution: Two replications of the Muir and Moray pasteurizer study find that dependability, not faith, is the earliest predictor of an operator's trust in process automation.
flag: agents per person: 1 - a single pasteurizer plant in which only the pump can be automated and the heating subsystem stays manual throughout; human measure: nine-construct trust questionnaire, performance score and proportion of time in automatic pump mode, all with condition contrasts and Bayes factors, so condition (1) is clearly met; excluded on condition (2) as single-agent supervisory control - the many-loops-of-one-plant-automation clause does not rescue it because only one loop is automated at all, though the maintainer may disagree since this is the classic process-plant supervisory paradigm.
