title: Agent transparency in mixed-initiative multi-UxV control: How should intelligent agent collaborators speak their minds?
venue: Computers in Human Behavior
evidence: Results 5.5: 'There was a significant main effect for Transparency, F (1,47) = 5.06, p = .029', whereby IAs that provided more transparency were trusted more; Method 3.2 has each operator managing six UxVs with an IA teammate
method: 2x2 mixed design varying SAT-model agent transparency (low, high) and IA face threat (complimentary, critical) in the FUSION multi-UxV mission-planning simulation with scripted IA advice
evaluation: 52 students, six simulated UxVs (2 UAV, 2 UGV, 2 USV) plus one IA advisor, 16 missions; trust F(1,47)=5.06 p=.029, mind changing F(1,50)=10.77 p=.002, reliance sensitivity A' F(1,50)=10.17 p=.002, plan accuracy 4.58-4.69 of 8 vs IA 5
contribution: Shows that how an intelligent agent phrases transparency - face threat and verbal vs graphical vs iconographic design - shifts multi-UxV operators' trust calibration and reliance, not only how much it discloses
flag: agents per person: 6 UxVs plus 1 IA advisor; human measure: trust (Lyons scale and Jian-style function trust), reliance sensitivity A', agreement, mind changing, plan-selection accuracy. No takeover and no time-critical handoff - this is advisory plan selection, so (e) holds only in the situation-awareness sense. Underpowered by the authors' own account (achieved power .73; 52 of the 62 planned participants) and most post-hoc contrasts are nonsignificant.

title: Overloaded, underloaded or in control: How many automated vehicles can one person supervise?
venue: Computers in Human Behavior
evidence: Results 4.2 and 4.4: NASA-TLX differed significantly between all four conditions (Car3 to Car5 Z=-3.100, p=.002; Car7 to Car9 Z=-2.798, p=.005) and SART Demand on Resources rose with AV count (chi2(3,24)=32.737, p<.001)
method: Within-subject simulator study isolating monitoring from interaction: participants monitored 3, 5, 7 or 9 simulated AVs in a Coventry-based suburban scenario and delegated any needed intervention to a separate remote driver
evaluation: 24 participants, four conditions (3/5/7/9 AVs); NASA-TLX chi2(3,24)=37.594 p<.001, events ignored chi2(3,24)=27.550 p<.001, calls to remote driver chi2(3,24)=32.923 p<.001 (110% of expected calls at Car3 falling sharply by Car9), median call time 22.7 s; authors put capacity near five AVs
contribution: Isolates pure monitoring from intervention to put a supervisory-capacity figure on remote AV oversight: workload and demand on resources rise monotonically with fleet size and useful capacity sits around five vehicles
flag: agents per person: 3, 5, 7 or 9 automated vehicles (fleet size is the manipulated factor); human measure: NASA-TLX, 3D-SART (Demand, Supply, Understanding), initial response time, events ignored, calls to remote driver. SA is SART only, no SAGAT, and SART is closer to workload than to SA; nonparametric tests throughout with n=24; the participant delegates to a remote driver rather than taking over control himself, so the handoff is a call for help rather than a takeover.

title: Human factor issues during remote ship monitoring tasks: An ecological lesson for system design in a distributed context
venue: International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics
evidence: Section 3.1 and 5.1: 'Six participants, with seafaring experience, were invited to conduct scenario-based simulation trials' as shore control centre operators monitoring up to six unmanned vessels, rated on a customised SART questionnaire (Table 4)
method: Remote supervisory-control prototype built on a full ship bridge system; four scenario-based trials (observation, action, automation failure, object identification) with deliberately injected automation and sensor failures
evaluation: 6 seafarers, up to six simulated unmanned cargo vessels, 4 scenarios each over three days; customised 9-item SART means by scenario (e.g. perceived difficulty 5.5 in Scenario 2 vs 4.8 in Scenario 4; interface-design item lowest at 4.0-4.3 throughout), plus interface-use frequency, alarm acknowledgement time and decision latency; no significance tests
contribution: An ecological reading of shore-based supervision of several unmanned ships, showing that interfaces lifted from the centralised bridge leave remote operators slow to notice injected automation failures
flag: agents per person: up to 6 unmanned vessels (Ship 1 to 6 carried primary and secondary tasks across the four scenarios); human measure: customised SART questionnaire plus alarm acknowledgement time and decision latency. EVALUATION FLOOR IS BORDERLINE - n=6, descriptive means and SDs contrasted across scenario conditions only, no inferential statistics and no per-condition latency figures in the text, so the maintainer may prefer exclude-E2. The abstract's 'objective performance' is only the action-compilation and interface-use counts in Figs 5 and 7.

title: Assessing situation awareness in multitasking supervisory control using success rate of self-terminating search
venue: International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics
evidence: Results Table 1: SAGAT situation-awareness accuracy 0.588 with the overview display vs 0.517 with the schematic display, F(1,17)=6.01, p=.016, and STVS success rate 0.1161 vs 0.0746, F(1,17)=36.38, p<.001, in the low-complexity condition
method: Eye-head integrated tracking study proposing the success rate of self-terminating visual search as an unobtrusive SA metric during a distributed process-control task (TWHITL plant simulator) performed concurrently with MATB-II
evaluation: 36 students split by display type (overview vs schematic) x scenario complexity (low, high), 9-min runs on days 4 and 5; SAGAT accuracy and STVS success rate as above, complexity effect F(1,17)=27.86 p<.001, STVS-SA correlation r=0.157 p=.021
contribution: Validates the success rate of self-terminating visual search, from combined eye and head tracking, as an unobtrusive proxy for SAGAT-measured situation awareness in multitasking supervisory control
flag: agents per person: many loops and indicators of one plant automation (VAC tower gauge panels, a fuel system of eight pumps and six tanks) plus three concurrent MATB-II subtasks - this counts only under the maintainer's ruling that a crew supervising many loops of one plant automation qualifies; there are no autonomous agents and no takeover of control. Human measure: SAGAT accuracy, STVS success rate, scan-path distance. MOST LIKELY OVERTURN of the includes if the ruling is read more narrowly (would then be exclude-E4).

title: Automation Transparency and Personalized Decision Support: Air Traffic Controller Interaction with a Resolution Advisory System
venue: IFAC-PapersOnLine
evidence: Method: 'Nine Swedish air traffic controller trainees' worked a sector containing 27 aircraft (19-22 present) and had 30 seconds to accept or reject each resolution advisory; Results give acceptance rates and transparency ratings.
method: Two interface representations (heading band vs more transparent solution-space diagram) crossed with strategically conformal vs nonconformal resolution advisories in an en-route conflict detection and resolution task.
evaluation: MUFASA real-time ATC simulator, 9 controller trainees, 2x2 within-subjects over a three-week protocol; 26 of 36 advisories accepted (72.2%), 77.8% conformal vs 66.7% nonconformal (Cochran's Q ns); Likert/VAS: solution-space view easier for combined solutions T=26 p=.040 r=.49 but more cluttered T=28 p=.014 r=.58.
contribution: Controllers accept personalised conflict-resolution advisories more often than nonconformal ones and rate a solution-space interface as more transparent but more cluttered, with no significant behavioural effect.
flag: agents per person: 19-22 aircraft in a sector under one resolution advisory system, the air-traffic-controller case the maintainer blessed; human measure: advisory acceptance rate, agreement rating, response time and Likert/VAS transparency and workload ratings; the behavioural manipulations were ALL non-significant (n=9 trainees, one designed conflict per run, so 36 advisory decisions in total) and the only significant results are questionnaire comparisons of the two interfaces, so the quantitative comparison that clears the floor is a subjective-rating contrast, not a performance one; also note the aircraft are flown by pilots, not automation - the single automation is the advisory system.

title: Attention allocation for human multi-robot control: Cognitive analysis based on behavior data and hidden states
venue: International Journal of Human Computer Studies
evidence: Section 3.5 and 4.1: participants ran a 15-minute session 'controlling 6 robots'; detected victims showed main effects of reliability F(1,44)=4.888, p=.032 and of queue mechanism F(1,44)=5.426, p=.024, and the operator 'needed to assume manual control to teleoperate' each failed robot
method: USARSim and MrCS multi-robot urban search task comparing a self-paced Open-queue showing all robots' self-reported conditions against a forced-paced shortest-job-first queue, crossed with imperfect self-diagnosis, plus a hidden Markov model of operator behaviour
evaluation: 48 students, 6 simulated P3-AT robots, 4 scripted robot failures requiring manual teleoperation takeover, reliability 90% vs 50%; victims detected F(1,44)=5.426 p=.024, victim finding and missing rates F(1,44)=5.976 p=.019, failures resolved, NASA-TLX, HMM emission and transition probabilities
contribution: Treats multi-robot supervision as a queue of robot-initiated interaction requests and shows that shortest-job-first scheduling of operator attention trades primary-task situation awareness against failures resolved, with hidden Markov states exposing the strategy shift
flag: agents per person: 6 robots; human measure: victim finding and missing rates (missing rate used as the SA proxy, no SAGAT), failures resolved, area explored, NASA-TLX, HMM cognitive states. Takeover is real: the operator assumes manual teleoperation of a failed robot. Imperfect automation (50% misdiagnosis) is manipulated. Interactions reported mostly as pairwise t-tests, several at p=.051-.059.

title: Human factor influences on supervisory control of remotely operated and autonomous vessels
venue: Ocean Engineering
evidence: Results and discussion: 'performance was reduced under conditions of (iii) supervising three vessels' - operators of three vessels had a 10% drop in track score (P=0.06) and a 3-s increase in handover time (P=0.01) compared with one vessel
method: Randomized 2^5 factorial simulator experiment on remote supervisory control varying skillset, passive monitoring time (5 vs 30 min), number of vessels (1 vs 3), available time (20 vs 60 s) and decision-support availability, across one handover and one takeover scenario
evaluation: 32 participants (gamers vs navigators), 1 vs 3 autonomous vessels; handover time, track score, collision outcome, boredom questionnaire; 3 vessels -10% track score P=0.06 and +3 s handover time P=0.01; with 20 s available time, 100% collisions after 5 min monitoring vs 50% after 30 min (BD interaction P=0.009)
contribution: Screens five human-factor influences on remote supervision of autonomous ships and shows that fleet size, the width of the critical time window and decision support, not operator background, drive handover and takeover performance
flag: agents per person: 1 or 3 autonomous vessels (fleet size is factor C); human measure: handover time, track score (percentage of an immediate control transfer), collision outcome, boredom questionnaire. Directly manipulates a 20-vs-60 s critical time window, which is the closest thing in this batch to time-to-irreversibility. Caveats: the authors call it a factor-screening design, and several headline effects sit at P=0.06 to 0.10 (including the 13% boredom track-score reduction at P=0.08).

title: Automated Decision Aids: When Are They Advisors and When Do They Take Control of Human Decision Making?
venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied
evidence: Method: 'On each trial, two aircraft appeared within the light gray circle' and participants judged that single pair with one automated decision aid; there is no fleet, team or multi-agent supervision anywhere in the task
method: Evidence-accumulation model fitted to choices and response times in an ATC conflict-detection task with manual, 75%-reliable and 95%-reliable decision-aid blocks, to test whether the aid acts as advisor or as an autonomous trigger
evaluation: 24 participants, 4,680 trials each (three blocks of 520 per session); accuracy and RT split by automation correctness, model parameters, Automation Trust Questionnaire; high-reliability aid directly drove evidence accumulation while the 75% aid was treated as an advisor and trusted less
contribution: Fits an evidence-accumulation model to show that operators treat a low-reliability decision aid as an advisor but let a high-reliability aid trigger their responses directly
flag: agents per person: 1 automated decision aid, with 2 aircraft stimuli per trial that are neither automated nor managed by the aid; human measure: accuracy, RT, evidence-accumulation parameters and subjective trust - condition (1) is met well and the modelling is strong. Excluded only on condition (2): a single aid giving advice on one aircraft pair at a time. The maintainer might try to read the ATC framing as the 'many aircraft under one automation' ruling, but only one pair is ever displayed and no arrival-management automation controls them.

title: Neuroergonomic evaluation of risk-warning eHMI penetration rates in vehicle platoons: effects on pedestrians’ mental workload, situation awareness, and gap acceptance
venue: Scientific Reports
evidence: Method: 24 participants 'simulated street-crossing decisions by selecting appropriate temporal gaps when encountering vehicle platoons' with SART and P300 measured; the pedestrian never supervises, monitors on behalf of, or takes over from the platoon
method: Video-based pedestrian crossing experiment with three risk-warning eHMI penetration rates (zero, partial, full) within AV platoons, randomized speeds and 2-6 s gaps, run with a concurrent auditory oddball task and 64-channel EEG
evaluation: 24 participants (18 retained for EEG), 5,112 vehicle encounters; 3D-SART, P300 amplitude at Cz, oddball counting accuracy and gap acceptance via GLMM; full eHMI penetration gave significantly higher SA and lower mental workload than zero penetration, partial penetration reduced crossing at eHMI-equipped vehicles
contribution: Neuroergonomic evidence that partial risk-warning eHMI adoption within AV platoons distorts pedestrian crossing behaviour, while full adoption raises situation awareness and lowers mental workload
flag: agents per person: a platoon of AVs, zero, half or all eHMI-equipped, so more than one automated entity is present; human measure: 3D-SART, P300 amplitude, oddball counting accuracy, gap acceptance. Excluded because the person is an external pedestrian, not a supervisor or operator: nothing is handed over or taken over and no automation defers to the person, so criterion (e) is not the subject. LIKELY OVERTURN - on a literal reading of condition (2) a pedestrian does monitor more than one automated vehicle, and the measured-human-outcome bar is cleared comfortably, so the maintainer may want this as include.

title: Human–automation interaction for multiple robot control: the effect of varying automation assistance and individual differences on operator performance
venue: Ergonomics
evidence: Table 2: SAGAT-style SA 70.7% correct (Manual) vs 76.0% (VS) vs 76.7% (VS+R), target detection 54.6% vs 65.3% vs 63.5% (Manual < VS p<.01, d=0.78) and NASA-TLX 69.09 vs 55.24 vs 47.49, F(2,28)=25.50, p<.001
method: Within-subject simulator experiment varying automation assistance level (Manual, automated vehicle spacing, spacing plus RoboLeader re-routing) while operators supervised a three-vehicle convoy, maintained 360-degree security and detected targets, with spatial ability and perceived attentional control as individual-difference factors
evaluation: 30 participants, 3-vehicle convoy (UAV, UGV and own manned ground vehicle) coordinated through the RoboLeader agent, three assistance levels, 30 targets per scenario; SA 70.7-76.7%, target detection 54.6% vs 65.3% d=0.78, A' 0.54 vs 0.65 p<.001, NASA-TLX F(2,28)=25.50 p<.001, fixation count and pupil diameter
contribution: Finds a moderate automation assistance level best for convoy supervision: target detection and workload improve with assistance while the highest level encourages complacent disengagement, with eye tracking exposing individual differences that subjective measures miss
flag: agents per person: 3 convoy vehicles (UAV, UGV and the operator's own manned ground vehicle) managed through the RoboLeader agent; human measure: SAGAT-style SA queries, target detection percentage and A', NASA-TLX, fixation count and pupil diameter. Note the main effect of assistance level on SA was NOT significant (Wilks lambda .94, F(2,28)=0.88) - SA differences appear only in interaction with spatial ability, so the abstract's 'maintaining situation awareness' claim is weaker than it reads. Complacency at the highest level is inferred from eye data, not directly measured.

title: Detecting automation failures in a simulated supervisory control environment
venue: Ergonomics
evidence: "Participants controlled three separate UAVs that were each searching different targets concurrently" and "each search feed had a different automation reliability rate: (1) 70% accurate, (2) 85% accurate, and (3) 95% accurate" (Sec. 2.4, Procedure); 96 participants, gaze and failure-detection measured.
method: Simulated multi-UAV supervisory control (SCOUT): three concurrent automated target-detection sensor feeds of differing reliability highlight targets, and the operator must click to correct automation misses and false alarms while doing chat and UAV-update side tasks.
evaluation: 96 participants, 3 automated displays (70/85/95% reliable), within-subject high vs low workload; missed-failure rate, combined human-automation accuracy, chat accuracy, crew status workload, pupil size, per-display dwell time; no latency reported.
contribution: Study of 96 operators monitoring three automated UAV sensor feeds of differing reliability, showing misses are missed about 2.5 times more often than false alarms and that attention is spread equally across displays (system-wide trust).
flag: agents per person: 3 UAVs, each with its own automated detection display; human measure: automation-failure detection, gaze dwell, pupil size and crew status workload - misses undetected about 2.5x more often than false alarms, detection worse under high workload for misses F(1,569)=96.2 p<.001 and false alarms F(1,570)=58.5 p<.001, no reliability main effect for misses F(2,569)=.661 p=.52, dwell about 33% per feed with no AOI main effect (low load F(2,1704)=1.3 p=.27), pupil larger under high load MDiff=.15 d=.61 p=.01. Check: the three displays are driven by one scripted automation on one operator station, which fits the maintainer's one-automation-many-entities ruling; degrees of freedom (569/570) are much larger than 96 participants, so the mixed-model unit of analysis should be checked.

title: Enhancing Situation Awareness in Multi-Robot Supervision: The Role of Adaptive Interfaces for Multiple Displays
venue: International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
evidence: "participants were instructed to supervise multiple robots through multiple displays" with four display scales of 3, 5, 7 and 9 robots and intervention required on deadlock or dynamic-obstacle events (Sec. 3.3, Task and procedure); SART and NASA-RTLX collected per condition.
method: VR multi-robot supervisory testbed where autonomously navigating robots stop on deadlock or obstacle events and the operator selects the robot's display and intervenes; baseline, dynamic and attention-based adaptive interfaces reorder or highlight displays.
evaluation: 30 participants, within-subject 3x4 design (baseline/dynamic/adaptive interface x 3/5/7/9 displays); completion time, event response time, gaze AOI ratio, NASA-RTLX, SART; two-way RM-ANOVA; no latency figures.
contribution: Controlled VR experiment with 30 operators showing multi-robot supervision degrades beyond five displays and that an attention-based adaptive interface restores situation awareness and lowers workload at every display count.
flag: agents per person: 3, 5, 7 or 9 autonomous robots, one display each; human measure: SART situation awareness, NASA-RTLX workload, task completion time, event response time and gaze AOI ratio - SART fell from 23.10 (3 displays) to 17.00 (9 displays) F(3,87)=23.395 p<0.001 and differed by interface F(2,58)=13.188 p<0.001 (baseline 17.72 lowest); workload rose with displays F(3,87)=33.276 p<0.001 (45.44 at 9) and was highest for baseline F(2,58)=11.563 p<0.001; completion time F(3,87)=5.865 p=0.001 and interface F(2,58)=4.727 p=0.013 with adaptive fastest (M=44.39 s); event response time F(3,87)=7.260 p<0.001, adaptive M=29.06 s. Check: SA is SART self-report plus AOI ratio, no SAGAT freeze probes (the authors say so in limitations), and the AOI gain may partly reflect cue-following.

title: Physiological Measures for Human Performance Analysis in Human-Robot Teamwork: Case of Tele-Exploration
venue: IEEE Access
evidence: "participants perform an aerial exploration using two robotic drones" and "participants monitor two drones; one always in autonomous mode, and the other one requires manual control after a while" (Sec. III, Experimental design); EEG, gaze, target detection and an eye-based SA metric recorded.
method: Simulated tele-exploration with a two-drone team; EEG workload and distraction indices plus gaze features (fixation rate, glance ratio, pupil size) are used to predict operator target detection, reaction time and a gaze-derived level-1 situation-awareness measure.
evaluation: 22 participants, 2 drones, 2x2x2x2 MANOVA (visual-search skill x multi-object-tracking skill x task type VS-VS vs MC-VS x task load); target detection, false detection, reaction time, eye-based SA, EEG workload and distraction; no latency.
contribution: User study with 22 operators of a two-drone team relating EEG and gaze measures to target detection and a real-time gaze-based situation-awareness metric, and showing that visual-skill individual differences moderate both.
flag: agents per person: 2 drones (one autonomous, one handed over to manual control mid-run); human measure: target detection, gaze-derived level-1 SA, reaction time, false detection, EEG mental workload and distraction, pupil size - switching from dual visual scanning to manual control plus scanning and raising task load significantly degraded target detection and SA (MANOVA and follow-up ANOVAs, Bonferroni alpha .0125/.0167/.025), visual-search skill affected target detection F(1,18)=7.4 p=.012 eta2p=.3 and multi-object-tracking skill affected SA F(1,18)=8.12 p=.011 eta2p=.31, task-load x MOT interaction on pupil size F(1,18)=8.3 p=.01. Check: the SA score is a bespoke gaze-timer formula validated only against the authors' own definition, not SAGAT or SART, and takeover to manual control is scripted rather than operator-initiated.

title: Experimental Design & Pilot Testing for ECLSS Anomaly Resolution using Daphne-AT Virtual Assistant
venue: 2021 IEEE Aerospace Conference (50100)
evidence: "Pilot testing was conducted during the Summer 2020 and included five male subjects" who resolved four ECLSS anomalies per session with and without the Daphne-AT virtual assistant (Sec. 7, Pilot testing and preliminary results); each subject supervises one spacecraft ECLSS through one assistant.
method: Daphne-AT virtual assistant that detects, diagnoses and recommends anomaly-resolution procedures for a simulated spacecraft environmental control and life support system, with chat and voice interfaces and a mission-control monitoring screen.
evaluation: 5 subjects, within-subject with vs without Daphne-AT over 4 anomalies per session, 18 scripted ECLSS anomaly scenarios; anomalies resolved, NASA-TLX, SART subscales, Jian trust scale; no inferential statistics, no latency.
contribution: Experimental design and five-subject pilot test of a spacecraft anomaly-resolution virtual assistant, reporting higher anomaly-resolution success, lower workload and higher reported attention when the assistant is available.
flag: agents per person: 1 virtual assistant supervising 1 spacecraft ECLSS (many subsystems and parameters, but one automated system and one controlled entity); human measure: anomalies resolved 3.2 +/- 0.37 with vs 2.0 +/- 0.70 without Daphne-AT, NASA-TLX total 57.2 +/- 5.78 vs 66 +/- 7.31, SART concentration of attention 4.8 +/- 0.66 vs 3 +/- 0.89, division of attention 2 +/- 0.45 vs 3 +/- 0.95, spare capacity 5 +/- 0.45 vs 3.8 +/- 0.97, Jian trust scale. MOST LIKELY OVERTURN in this batch: the human outcome and the condition contrast are there, so the only ground for exclusion is the single-agent level; ECLSS is a life-support plant whose many loops the crew monitors under one automation, which can be read as satisfying the maintainer's plant-crew ruling. Also note n=5, no statistics, and SART reported only as individual subscales.

title: Enhancing Scalable Autonomy Space Teleoperation with User Intervention During Task Execution
venue: 2026 IEEE Aerospace Conference
evidence: "a user study was conducted with 24 participants" who performed the sample-container task under autonomous, intervention and free-choice conditions and rated usefulness and time pressure on Likert scales (Sec. 6, Results); only divergence bar plots of opinion and free-text suggestions are reported.
method: Scalable-autonomy telerobotic interface for an orbit-to-ground robot team: a cancellation button (method 1) or haptic deadzone and force-reflection intent detection (method 2) lets the operator interrupt autonomous execution and take over by direct teleoperation.
evaluation: ISS-to-ground Surface Avatar session (one astronaut, single run: 4.23 s autonomous then 76.87 s teleoperation after takeover) plus a 24-participant two-robot ground study with three conditions reporting only Likert opinion distributions; method 2 shown in simulation only.
contribution: Describes and demonstrates cancellation-based and haptic-intent-based operator intervention during autonomous space telerobotic task execution, with an ISS demonstration and a 24-participant study of perceived usefulness and time pressure.
flag: agents per person: a heterogeneous robot team (Justin, Rollin Justin, Bert, Spot per Table 1) in the ISS session, 2 robots in the user study; human measure: Likert ratings of intervention usefulness and perceived time pressure and of visual/haptic/audio assistance, plus coded free-text suggestions - reported only as divergence bar plots (for example 5 participants completely disagreed about added time pressure), with no per-condition quantitative human result; the only timing figures (4.23 s autonomous, 76.87 s teleoperation, 1 min 35 s total) come from the single astronaut run, not from the 24 participants. Excluded on the evaluation floor, not on the setting; if the maintainer counts the Likert distributions as a quantitative human outcome with a condition contrast, this becomes an include.

title: Experiments of human-robot teaming under sliding autonomy
venue: 2016 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics (AIM)
evidence: "one expert user and one novice user each performed ten trials under every control mode" for a three-robot site-clearing task, with "data on completion time (in seconds), solution quality and operator" workload via NASA TLX (Sec. IV.A, Simulation results); robots request help and the operator can intervene at any time.
method: Sliding-autonomy control of a multi-robot team with autonomy, system-initiative, mixed-initiative, teleoperation and a new peer-to-peer mode, where either a robot (error detection) or the operator can trigger a switch of control.
evaluation: USARSim simulation of 3 robots clearing a site, 1 expert and 1 novice operator, 10 trials per control mode, plus a physical two-robot iRobot Create demonstration; completion time, solution quality, NASA-TLX; no latency.
contribution: Extends sliding autonomy to a multi-robot team with a peer-to-peer mode and reports completion time, solution quality and operator workload across four control modes in simulation and on physical robots.
flag: agents per person: 3 simulated robots (2 physical robots in the hardware demonstration); human measure: NASA-TLX workload with completion time and solution quality per control mode, experienced vs novice operator - autonomy 176 s/72%/TLX 0 vs 0, system-initiative 189 vs 176 s/96% vs 95%/TLX 34 vs 31, mixed-initiative 180 vs 176 s/100% vs 98%/TLX 52 vs 34, teleoperation 253 vs 241 s/100%/TLX 62 vs 43. Check: only two operators and no statistics, the authors themselves call the workload data "very subjective", and the physical peer-to-peer mode was only partly demonstrated because a second robot was unavailable.

title: Measurement of Situational Awareness in the Supervisory Tasks
venue: 2018 Innovations in Intelligent Systems and Applications Conference (ASYU)
evidence: "experiments were performed with 30 participants (engineers) aged 23-47" split into three groups of 10 by notification design, each running two 20-minute air-traffic scenarios containing 5 and 10 alarm situations (Sec. II.A, Katilimcilar, and Sec. II.C); verification time and completed-task count measured.
method: Three peripheral alarm notification designs (red label font, red label background, and a gaze-positioned notification window driven by a Tobii X2-30 eye tracker) layered on an operational air-traffic-control radar simulator.
evaluation: 30 participants, between-groups notification design (n=10 each) x 2 scenarios (5 vs 10 alarms) on the atcTRsim ATC radar simulator; alarm verification time and number of completed primary tasks; two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc; no latency.
contribution: Compares three peripheral alarm notification designs on an air-traffic-control radar simulator, showing background-colour and gaze-positioned window alerts give faster alarm verification and more completed primary tasks than font colour alone.
flag: agents per person: many aircraft on one ATC radar under one conflict-alert automation (5 or 10 alarm situations per 20-minute scenario), which fits the maintainer's controller-with-many-aircraft ruling; human measure: alarm verification time (SA proxy) and number of completed primary tasks - notification design main effect on verification time F(2,54)=73.139 p<.001 (background colour and notification window both significantly faster than red font, no difference between them), no design x scenario interaction F(2,60)=0.980 p=.382 and no scenario effect F(1,60)=0.995 p=.323; completed tasks main effect F(2,60)=18.733 p<0.05 with background colour 189, notification window 180, red font 164. Check: the paper's body is in Turkish, the aircraft count per scenario is never stated (only alarm counts), participants are engineers rather than licensed controllers, and the reported ANOVA degrees of freedom are inconsistent between the two tables (54 vs 60 error df).

title: Expert-based design and evaluation of an ambient light display to improve monitoring performance during multi-UAV supervisory control
venue: 2015 IEEE International Multi-Disciplinary Conference on Cognitive Methods in Situation Awareness and Decision
evidence: "We invited 3 experts from 2 different departments of the UAV manufacturer" to test the ambient light display prototype individually in three 10-minute phases, after which "each expert answered the questionnaire" of 15 Likert statements (Sec. V, Evaluation); only agreement ratings are reported.
method: Ambient light display that continuously externalises a multi-UAV commander's monitoring-behaviour adequacy as peripheral brightness and colour cues, derived from eye-tracked attendedness and situation relevance per UAV and designed in an expert sketching workshop.
evaluation: Expert design workshop (4 experts) plus expert evaluation with 3 UAV-domain experts on a multi-UAV microworld with eye tracking; outcome is mean Likert agreement per statement, requirement and category (for example R.1 M=4, SD=0.45); no objective performance measure and no control condition.
contribution: Expert-based design and expert walkthrough evaluation of an ambient peripheral light display intended to make a multi-UAV commander's own monitoring performance visible without adding workload.
flag: agents per person: multiple UAVs in the microworld (exact number not stated); human measure: none objective - only 3 experts' subjective Likert agreement with statements about usefulness, obtrusiveness, intention to use and "the ALD increases my workload", with no monitoring-performance, gaze or workload-instrument data and no baseline condition; the authors state that "larger pools of participants and objective measures are indispensable". Excluded under the ruling's bar on acceptance and usefulness surveys about a technology; if the maintainer treats the inverted workload item as a workload measure it would still fail the evaluation floor for lack of a condition contrast.

title: Human interactive machine learning for trust in teams of autonomous robots
venue: 2017 IEEE Conference on Cognitive and Computational Aspects of Situation Management, CogSIMA 2017
evidence: "Sixty participants were recruited" and, after training the search behaviours of a three-robot team, "made a response, 1-100 on a sliding trust scale" while choosing between interactive-ML and black-box team plans and labelling their origin (Sec. IV, Experiment, and Sec. V, Initial results).
method: Interactive machine learning in which the operator steers neuroevolution of area-search behaviours for a three-robot team every 10 or 25 evolution steps, compared against non-interactive neuroevolved (black box) plans of matched fitness.
evaluation: 60 participants, 3-robot simulated area search; IML vs fitness-matched black-box plans, counterbalanced 10-step vs 25-step human input; plan choice proportion, 1-100 trust rating, plan-origin labelling accuracy over 80 trials; no latency.
contribution: Shows that letting operators steer the evolution of a robot team's search behaviours makes the resulting plans more often chosen and recognisable, yet slightly less trusted than opaque neuroevolved plans.
flag: agents per person: a team of 3 autonomous robots whose search behaviours the participant shapes and then judges; human measure: plan choice proportion M=.66 SD=.16 overall and 71.5% vs 60% for the 25-step-first counterbalance F(1,44)=5.93 p=.02 eta2p=.12, 1-100 trust rating higher for black-box (M=63) than IML (M=60) plans F(1,34)=6.5 p=.02 eta2p=.16 and higher with less human involvement F(1,34)=4.9 p=.04 eta2p=.13, labelling accuracy M=.77. Check: the human role is offline plan selection, trust rating and labelling, not runtime supervision, intervention or takeover, so criterion (e) holds only through the trust and transparency route; effects are small, the authors call them possibly not operationally significant, and some participants were dropped for missing data (df 34 and 44 from 60 recruited).

title: SAHRTA: A Supervisory-Based Adaptive Human-Robot Teaming Architecture
venue: 2020 IEEE Conference on Cognitive and Computational Aspects of Situation Management (CogSIMA)
evidence: "A total of eighteen participants completed the trial in either a No Adaptation condition or in one of three adaptation conditions" on a physically expanded NASA MATB-II (Sec. V, Pilot study); the evaluation task is one simulated aircraft's four subtasks, not a robot team.
method: SAHRTA architecture that estimates five workload components and predicted future performance in real time from physiological and behavioural features and then adapts the supervisory interface's autonomy level or interaction modality per task.
evaluation: 18 participants (10 no-adaptation, 8 adaptive) on a physically expanded NASA MATB-II with underload/normal/overload blocks; tracking RMSE, resource-management time in range, system-monitoring reaction time and success, NASA-TLX, in-situ workload (Mann-Whitney); no latency figures.
contribution: Introduces a supervisory adaptive architecture that selects autonomy level or interaction modality from a multi-dimensional real-time workload estimate and predicted performance, and pilot-tests it on an expanded multi-attribute task battery.
flag: agents per person: 1 automated station (four MATB-II subtasks of a single simulated aircraft: tracking, system monitoring, resource management, communications); no robots were used despite the human-robot teaming title; human measure: estimated workload and task performance, adaptation vs no adaptation - overall workload estimate 39.76 (SD 6.65) with vs 44.04 (5.07) without adaptation in overload, cognitive 12.77 vs 15.56, tracking RMSE 126.14 (Both) and 115.84 (Autonomy) vs 200.28 (None) in overload, resource-management time in range 99% (Interaction) vs 68% (None), system-monitoring reaction time 4.52-5.83 s vs 6.25 s, plus NASA-TLX and in-situ ratings with a Mann-Whitney test. Excluded on level, not on measurement; the maintainer may want to decide whether four concurrently automated subtasks of one station count as the plant-many-loops case, and note n=10 vs 8 between-groups with mostly descriptive statistics.

title: A Dynamic Bayesian Network and Markov Decision Process for Tactical UAV Decision Making in MUM-T Scenarios
venue: 2022 IEEE Conference on Cognitive and Computational Aspects of Situation Management (CogSIMA)
evidence: "We evaluated TacARA in an experimental setup with 12 participants and different snapshots of tactical situations" (Sec. IV, Experiments and Discussion); the measured quantity is agreement between agent and operator, not an operator outcome.
method: TacARA assistance agent for manned-unmanned teaming: a Dynamic Bayesian Network scores threat of enemy units and a Markov Decision Process proposes UAV reconnaissance tasks or helicopter route re-planning to the crew.
evaluation: 12 participants judged 6 static tactical snapshots blind, then 7 snapshots with TacARA output shown; outcome is operator-agent agreement (77% threat assessment, 71% actions); no baseline condition, no workload, SA or takeover measure, no latency.
contribution: Threat-assessment and UAV-tasking agent for helicopter crews whose proposals match human operators' own threat ratings and tasking choices in most of 13 tactical snapshots.
flag: agents per person: 2-3 UAVs plus 1-3 enemy units in each snapshot, with the crew tasking the UAVs. human measure: none proper - only agent-human agreement rate (77% threat assessment, 71% tactical action) plus an unquantified remark that participants "felt safer" and "felt to have a better situation awareness"; no SA score, workload, trust or takeover metric, no condition contrast, and the humans serve as the reference standard for validating the agent rather than being the measured object. Maintainer may want to overturn: there ARE participants and percentages, and the authors call for SA study as future work, so if agent-human agreement counts as a human outcome this becomes an include on multi-agent grounds. Also note the task is paper-like snapshots, not a real-time simulation, so no takeover event exists.

title: Supporting Situation Awareness in Multi-Platform Anomaly Detection: From Theory to Application
venue: 2026 IEEE Conference on Cognitive and Computational Aspects of Situation Management, CogSIMA 2026
evidence: "Although this activity did not constitute formal user testing or a controlled field study, it enabled early feedback elicitation to inform subsequent design iterations" (Sec. III.C, Expert User Feedback Elicitation).
method: TRACE prototype human-machine interface (Grafana dashboard with anomaly tracker, anomaly timeline, UAS tracker, telemetry plots and map) for telemetry-based anomaly detection over a drone swarm, derived from cognitive work analysis and five stated SA challenges.
evaluation: Unity simulation of a 5-drone swarm with scripted GPS spoofing and jamming; interface driven by a researcher and demonstrated to subject-matter experts over two days; only narrative SME themes reported, no participant count, no metrics, no conditions.
contribution: Cognitive-systems-engineering analysis of five situation-awareness challenges in swarm anomaly detection, with a telemetry dashboard prototype and design implications drawn from expert walkthroughs.
flag: agents per person: 5 simulated drones in one swarm (paper also cites 3-8 drone collectives as the near-term norm). human measure: none - no SA score, workload, trust or response-time measure; the HMI was operated by a researcher, not by participants, and SME reactions are reported only as themes. Design concept plus informal feedback, which the maintainer's rule (1) excludes explicitly. Poster-track paper; AI/ML development and evaluation are stated out of scope.

title: Effects of transparency on pilot trust and agreement in the autonomous constrained flight planner
venue: 2016 IEEE/AIAA 35th Digital Avionics Systems Conference (DASC)
evidence: "12 commercial transport pilots ... were given six time-pressured all land scenarios where they needed to use the ACFP to determine diversions for multiple aircraft" (Sec. II.A-B, Method); "there was a statistically significant effect of Transparency on trust, F (2, 22) = 4.39, p < 0.05" (Sec. III.A).
method: Autonomous Constrained Flight Planner recommends diversion airport and runway with risk estimates to a ground super-dispatcher; transparency is varied additively over three levels (Baseline recommendation, Value success probability, Logic reasoning statements).
evaluation: High-fidelity NASA Ames ground station, 12 transport-rated pilots, within-subject 3x2 Transparency x Risk, 6 aircraft per scenario; trust scale (alpha 0.88-0.92), verification, exploration and agreement probabilities; non-parametric tests; no latency or hardware figures.
contribution: Human-in-the-loop study showing that increasing automation transparency raises ground operators' trust in a diversion planner and lowers their need to verify its recommendations for multiple aircraft at once.
flag: agents per person: 6 aircraft per scenario, each with an ACFP diversion recommendation from one central planner, which is the maintainer's one-automation-many-entities case. human measure: trust (7-item scale, significant effect of transparency F(2,22)=4.39, p<0.05, highest in Logic and lowest in Baseline) plus behavioural verification (Baseline 62%-65% vs Value and Logic 28%-44%, Friedman p=0.015), exploration (Low Risk Baseline 74% vs Value 38% and Logic 37%, p=0.018; main effect of Risk p=0.006) and agreement (High Risk 73%-86% vs Low Risk 79%-95%, Wilcoxon p=0.046). Things to check: the trust means in Fig. 3 are taken from a companion paper [18] rather than analysed here, so the only trust statistic in this paper is second-hand; agreement data were strongly skewed and the authors admit their non-parametric tests could not detect the Transparency x Risk interaction they then interpret; the pilots played a ground-operator role that does not exist, and no takeover event or SA score is measured, so (e) rests on trust and reliance behaviour.

title: Human Machine Interface Design to Support Safety Risk Monitoring of Autonomous Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems – Results from a Mock-Up Evaluation
venue: 2021 IEEE/AIAA 40th Digital Avionics Systems Conference (DASC)
evidence: "Results from a first analysis related to operator performance, situation awareness and workload showed positive findings [15]. This paper focusses on the usability and acceptability of the designed HMI" (Sec. II).
method: Icon-based ground control station HMI that visualises high-level states of geo-fencing, collision avoidance and health monitoring for eight autonomous small UAS in low-altitude urban airspace, hiding sub-system detail until a UAS or function is selected.
evaluation: Online mock-up study, 7 UAS pilots, three static and one dynamic scenario with 8 UAS and scripted off-nominal events; measures are SUS 75.35 (SD 3.94), general acceptability 3.57 (SD 1.27), Technology Acceptance usefulness 1.43 and satisfiability 1.42; no conditions compared.
contribution: Mock-up evaluation of an icon-based interface for supervising eight autonomous urban UAS, reporting satisfactory usability and acceptability alongside operators' concerns about hidden sub-system detail.
flag: agents per person: 8 UAS monitored by one pilot, two of them in off-nominal states per scenario. human measure: only usability and acceptance questionnaires (SUS 75.35, acceptability 3.57, TAS 1.43 and 1.42), which the maintainer's rule (1) excludes as attitude or acceptance surveys; there is no condition contrast and a single mock-up. Maintainer should note the interesting but unquantified observation from screen and voice recordings that most participants would have intervened earlier than the automation did in the mitigation events - a takeover-timing finding reported with no numbers. The operator performance, situation awareness and workload results for the same HMI live in the companion paper Friedrich and Vollrath (Aerospace 8(3), 2021, ref [15]); if that paper is not already in the pool it is the one worth screening.

title: A Human-In-The-Loop Simulation for Urban Air Mobility in the Terminal Area
venue: AIAA/IEEE Digital Avionics Systems Conference - Proceedings
evidence: "Although limited findings for this study will not be reported as the study has not yet been executed, the authors conclude with potential outcomes" (Abstract); Sec. VI gives only "Expected Results" with notional trend figures.
method: Proposed design for a human-in-the-loop simulation in which a vertiport manager spaces UAM arrival traffic by speed instruction only, aided by three levels of automation: none, spacing-violation detection, and detection plus speed-adjustment recommendation.
evaluation: Not executed: a 3x3 repeated-measures design (levels of automation x 0, 1, 2 min airborne error) is proposed with throughput, delay, loss of separation, NASA-TLX, SART and a Korber trust questionnaire; all result figures are predicted trends, no participants recruited.
contribution: Experiment design proposal for measuring a vertiport manager's throughput, delay, workload, situation awareness and trust under three levels of arrival-spacing automation in midterm urban air mobility.
flag: agents per person: not yet determined - the proposed arrival stream is a single flow of highly automated UAM vehicles spaced at 45 s by one demand-capacity-balancing system, so the setting would qualify once run. human measure: none measured; NASA-TLX, SART and a trust questionnaire are only recommended, and every reported figure is an expected trend drawn by the authors. Protocol or study-design paper with no data at all, so exclude is not borderline; the maintainer may want to track the eventual results paper from the same NASA group.

title: Rethinking the Role of the Operator: A Case Study of Human-Machine Teaming for Wheel Loader Fleet Operation
venue: Conference on Human System Interactions
evidence: "we present a wheel-loader case study involving semi-autonomous fleet operation of 3 wheel loaders by a single operator" (Abstract); "all participants perceived semi-autonomous fleet operation to be less stressful compared to manual operation of a single wheel loader" (Sec. IV.B, Human Factors Evaluation).
method: Semi-autonomous fleet concept where one operator manually fills the bucket of each wheel loader and then hands control to an autonomous driving agent that secures the bucket, drives, dumps and returns, letting the operator switch to the next machine.
evaluation: Mevea physics simulator with a motion-platform operator station, 6 participants, within-subject order manual-auto-auto-manual, 7 min runs; productivity 9.53 t vs 3.77 t (about 2.5x), fuel productivity 3.39 vs 1.98 t/L (about 1.7x), perceived stress 1-10 and trust per participant; no statistics, no latency.
contribution: Simulator case study in which one operator loading three semi-autonomous wheel loaders in turn roughly doubled productivity and fuel productivity while reporting lower stress than manual single-machine operation.
flag: agents per person: 3 wheel loaders with one autonomous driving agent each in fleet mode versus 1 machine in the manual baseline, with an explicit control handover at the end of each loading cycle and an operator takeover when the machine returns. human measure: perceived stress on a 1-10 scale (manual 8,7,6,7,6,7 vs semi-autonomous 5,4,3,4,2,4 for S1-S6, i.e. about 6.8 vs 3.7), self-reported trust in autonomy 7-10, and operator task performance (9.53 t vs 3.77 t transported, 3.39 vs 1.98 t/L). Things to check: N=6, no inferential statistics or effect sizes anywhere, and the authors themselves file the stress and trust ratings under qualitative feedback (Table I) rather than a validated instrument - no NASA-TLX, no SA measure, despite the paper arguing situation awareness is the open question. The productivity comparison is also 3 machines versus 1, so the gain partly reflects machine count rather than the interface. Environment was obstacle-free with predefined routes and no automation failures, so no genuine contingency takeover was tested.

title: Multi-presence System with Local Augmented Body - Investigation of human cognitive limitation and spatial awareness in teleoperation
venue: 2024 IEEE-RAS 23rd International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids)
evidence: "The analysis revealed a statistically significant difference in task performance scores, chi2 = 13.5, p = 0.001" for 2 vs 3 vs 4 robots (Sec. III.A); "For the 4-robot condition with assistance, the median (IQR) time taken was 3.7 (2.9 to 4.2). In contrast, without assistance, the median (IQR) time was 16.8 (14.8 to 22.0)" (Sec. III.D).
method: Multi-presence telepresence system: four-way split-screen head-mounted display over up to four 3-DoF robotic heads in separate rooms, with an optional assistance mode that voice-notifies the operator which room needs attention.
evaluation: 12 participants, within-subject sweep of robot number (2, 3, 4), task number (2, 3) and difficulty (easy, hard) plus an assistance on/off contrast at 4 robots; scored detection performance and LED detection time; Friedman and Wilcoxon with Bonferroni; OpenCR1.0 and ROS, no latency figures.
contribution: User study locating the cognitive threshold of multi-robot telepresence at three robots, and showing that automated attention cueing cuts detection time at four robots from 16.8 s to 3.7 s.
flag: agents per person: 2, 3 or 4 telepresence robots, one per room, controlled by a single operator through a split-screen HMD. human measure: task performance score (medians 4.3 for 2 robots, 7.0 for 3 robots, 0.3 for 4 robots; Friedman chi2=13.5, p=0.001; 3 vs 4 robots Z=-3.059, p=0.002; 2 vs 4 Z=-2.589, p=0.01), difficulty effect at 4 robots (Z=-2.118, p=0.034), and LED detection time with versus without automated voice assistance (median 3.7 s vs 16.8 s, Z=-3.061, p=0.002, while the concurrent ball-task score did not improve significantly, Z=-1.490, p=0.136). Things to check: the paper talks throughout about cognitive load but never measures it - no NASA-TLX, no physiological or gaze measure - so load is inferred from performance alone, and the abstract's claim that three robots minimise cognitive load is not supported by any load measurement. The robots are teleoperated heads rather than autonomous agents; the only automation that defers to the person is the assistance-mode notification, which is where (e) comes from. 11 of 12 participants were male laboratory members, and the task is an abstract ball and LED search.

title: Hitting the Road: Exploring Human-Robot Trust for Self-Driving Vehicles
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Human-Machine Systems, ICHMS 2020
evidence: "Twenty-nine participants took part in our human-in-the-loop driving simulator experiment" and the self-driving cars were other road users at four-way stops, "programmed to behave exactly the same" as human-driven cars (Sec. III-IV); the participant drives a single manual vehicle and supervises nothing.
method: Exploratory factor analysis of a shortened Jian Standard Trust Scale against Mayer's Ability, Integrity and Benevolence dimensions, tested in a Unity and AirSim driving simulator where the participant meets labelled self-driving or human-driven cars at intersections.
evaluation: 29 participants, in-house immersive simulator, within-subject comparison of car category (self-driving vs human-driven) over 8 intersections; EFA (KMO 0.83, 3 factors, 57% variance) and linear mixed models; Ability raised 4.7 +/- 2.2% for human-driven cars, chi2(1)=4.27, p=0.041.
contribution: Driving-simulator study validating a three-dimension trust scale and exposing an anti-automation bias: identically behaving cars are judged less able and more irritating when labelled self-driving.
flag: agents per person: not a supervisory setting - the participant manually drives one car and merely encounters about 6 labelled self-driving vehicles as fellow road users at four-way stops; there is no fleet, no supervision, no monitoring task and no handoff, and the automation never defers to the person. human measure: trust is properly measured (Standard Trust Scale, Ability affected by car category chi2(1)=4.27, p=0.041, 4.7 +/- 2.2%; Fisher exact tests on trustworthiness p=0.025 and irritation p=0.022; familiarity Wilcoxon p=0.02), so condition (1) of the ruling is satisfied and only condition (2) fails, hence E4 rather than E2. The maintainer could equally call this E1, since criterion (e) is not the subject at all: this is a bystander trust-perception and scale-validation paper. Sample skews young and male (76% aged 18-22, 79% men) and several a priori correlations fell below significance after FDR adjustment.

title: sUAS Ground Control Station Capabilities Impact on Fleet Management
venue: 2024 IEEE 4th International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS)
evidence: "each subject played the role of a Pilot-in-Command responsible for managing the operations of a fleet of 28 highly automated sUAS vehicles tasked with delivering packages" (Sec. III, Experimental Design); workload was collected with the NASA TLX and maneuver and response times logged per trial (Sec. IV).
method: Three ground control station configurations for fleet management of 28 automated delivery sUAS: Manual waypoint editing only, Auto quick plays (emergency land, loiter, return to base) only, and Hybrid adding a Propagate play that copies one reroute to further vehicles.
evaluation: 12 Part 107 pilots, modified Vigilant Spirit Control Station, 3x2x3 within-subject (GCS configuration x airspace density x 2-4 vehicles affected by a UAS Volume Reservation), 18 five-minute trials; NASA-TLX, maneuver and response time, maneuver type, warning-state rate; descriptive only.
contribution: Fleet-management study showing that a ground station mixing manual rerouting with automated plays keeps workload and response time near the fully automated station while producing better mission-preserving decisions.
flag: agents per person: 28 highly automated sUAS per pilot-in-command, with 2-4 of them affected by each airspace reservation. human measure: NASA-TLX workload (lowest for Auto, highest for Manual; higher in high-density trials; plateauing beyond two affected vehicles; Auto lowest at 2 affected vehicles, Hybrid lowest at 4), response time (Auto 66.4 s, Hybrid 75.9 s, Manual 84.2 s; high density 83.3 s vs low 69.2 s; 2, 3, 4 affected vehicles 58.0 s, 75.5 s, 86.0 s), chosen maneuver leading to a warning state 7.3% of the time, and preference (11 of 12 ranked Hybrid first). Things to check: not one inferential statistic or variance estimate is reported anywhere - all claims rest on means and figure trends - and the stated conclusion that Hybrid keeps workload and response times similar to Auto is therefore untested; situation awareness is asserted from a post-block agreement item (97% agreeing the displays gave sufficient SA) rather than a SAGAT or SART measure; and data from an unspecified number of trials were dropped for extreme system lag.

title: Human-Autonomy Teaming Assistant to Support Small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems for Wildland Firefighting Operations
venue: 2024 IEEE 4th International Conference on Human-Machine Systems (ICHMS)
evidence: "the ability of a remote pilot in command (RPIC) to manage four sUAS on a transect mission ... were tested across two different GCS Modes (Assisted and Unassisted) with two levels of Complexity" (Sec. I); "participants were generally faster and more consistent at responding to the presented contingency events in the Assisted Mode than the Unassisted Mode" (Sec. V.D).
method: Human-Autonomy Teaming Assistant in a ground control station: a chat-based agent that posts a 0-100 mission risk value with sparkline trend, answers why on request, and preselects a mitigating play (return to base, reconfigure asset, emergency land) once risk reaches 50.
evaluation: 10 Part 107 pilots, modified Vigilant Spirit Control Station, within-subject 2x2 (Assisted vs Unassisted x Low vs High Complexity), four 15-min trials, 4 sUAS; NASA-TLX, SART, Merritt trust, response times T1-T5, play-execution counts; all subjective contrasts null.
contribution: Exploratory simulation of a risk-alerting teaming assistant for an operator of four firefighting sUAS: workload, situation awareness and trust were unchanged, but contingency detection and response were markedly faster.
flag: agents per person: 4 sUAS per remote pilot in command on a wildland-fire transect mission, with contingencies affecting one asset (Low Complexity battery drain) or all assets (High Complexity weather inversion). human measure: NASA-TLX (Assisted 20.93 SE 2.33 vs Unassisted 22.37 SE 2.55), SART (27.25 SE 2.47 vs 27.40 SE 2.02), Merritt trust (4.55 SE 0.22 vs 4.33 SE 0.25) - all non-significant; the only significant test is the post-block item that the GCS gave sufficient SA, Assisted 4.7 vs Unassisted 4.0, F(1,9)=5.4, p=0.045; response time T1 18.17 s Assisted vs 76.25 s Unassisted and T3 38.89 s vs 80.25 s; detection behaviour 10 of 10 executing a play in Assisted versus 2 of 10 in Unassisted Low Complexity and 5 of 10 in Unassisted High Complexity. Things to check: the response-time cells rest on N=2 to N=5 participants because most unassisted operators never noticed the event, so the headline speed advantage is a comparison of self-selected responders and is reported with no test; the authors state hypothesis testing was not the objective and that SART may lack sensitivity here; and they flag that participants may have rated trust in the whole ground station rather than in the assistant.

title: The impact of automated planning aids on situation awareness and workload in the monitoring of uncrewed vehicles
venue: 2024 IEEE 4th International Conference on Human-Machine Systems, ICHMS 2024
evidence: Method: 'Each trial included route planning (phase one) and monitoring (phase two) for two UVs'; participants intervened when UVs approached unsafe areas, with SAGAT freeze probes and NASA-TLX per block (Measures).
method: Virtual uncrewed-vehicle monitoring task with an automated route planner at three levels of automation (generation and selection traded between operator and system), between groups across three blocks.
evaluation: 44 participants, 3 LOA groups x 3 blocks of 22 trials, 2 UVs per trial, EyeLink II gaze; SAGAT 44% correct (SE 1.8%); TLX 34.1, 34.5, 30.8 by block F(1.89,77.6)=11.35 p<0.001; search performance by group F(2,41)=3.42 p=0.042.
contribution: Shows that varying the level of automation of a route planner changes neither situation awareness nor workload in a two-vehicle monitoring task, while task experience does.
flag: agents per person: 2 uncrewed vehicles monitored per trial; human measure: SAGAT situation-awareness score, NASA-TLX, gaze-based visual attention and monitoring/search performance; the headline manipulation (LOA) was null - the significant effects are block (practice) effects and one between-group search-performance difference that was already significant at baseline, which the authors concede; multi-agent only just clears the two-or-more bar.

title: Testing Operating Procedures for Large UAS with Detect and Avoid Capabilities in Civil Air Traffic Management Environments
venue: 2023 Integrated Communication, Navigation and Surveillance Conference (ICNS)
evidence: One remote pilot supervised ONE large UAS (SkyGuardian) with DAA; human measures were NASA-TLX-based workload and Eurocontrol SASHA SA, scored 1-5 per scenario: 'Questions were based on the well-known NASA TLX workload metric, and the Eurocontrol SASHA methodology for measuring SA' (Sec. VI, footnote 2); no numeric scores appear in the body.
method: Human-in-the-loop ATC simulation (NARSIM plus MUST control station) of one SkyGuardian UAS with Class 2 plus Class 5 Detect and Avoid, TCAS II auto-executed RAs and CAVS delegated separation, in Rotterdam airspace.
evaluation: 10 scenarios, one professional per role (remote pilot, tower, approach, en-route controller) plus pseudo-pilots; workload, SA, safety and acceptability rated 1-5 versus a baseline scenario, but scores shown only in bar-chart figures, no numbers reported.
contribution: Human-in-the-loop ATC simulations of one large UAS with Detect and Avoid, yielding procedural recommendations for remote-pilot and controller coordination during DAA alerts and lost C2 link.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one UAS per remote pilot; background traffic was flown by human pseudo-pilots, not by a central automation). human measure: NASA-TLX-style workload and SASHA SA, 1-5 ratings. Genuinely single-agent: the paper's own future work lists 'Operations with multiple UAS in same airspace' as not yet done, so condition (2) fails. Evaluation floor also fails: n=1 per role and all rating scores appear only in figures (Fig. 13 etc.), no figure is quoted in text, so exclude-E2 would be defensible too. Controller supervises many aircraft but they are human-piloted, not one central automation.

title: Evaluation of Technology Concepts for Traffic data Management and Relevant audio for Datalink in Commercial Airline Flight Decks
venue: Integrated Communications, Navigation and Surveillance Conference (ICNS)
evidence: Experiment Plan: '12 Crews (24 pilots), two days per crew' in a 737-800 flight simulator; Results give overall NASA-TLX by traffic-data-manager filter condition and time to first reaction.
method: Flight-deck technology concepts: a traffic data manager filtering ADS-B traffic at three levels (static, dynamic, noisy) plus a 'conversational co-pilot' relaying relevant party-line audio for datalink clearances.
evaluation: Human-in-the-loop 737-800 simulator, 12 crews (24 pilots), 4 runs each across blown-tire, traffic and weather off-nominal events; overall NASA-TLX 35.4, 32.5, 33.3 across the three filter conditions (no significant difference); time to first reaction significant for the dynamic filter; SUS 63-80+.
contribution: Simulator evaluation of traffic-data filtering and relevant-audio concepts for datalink flight decks, finding no workload penalty and faster crew reaction with the dynamic traffic filter.
flag: agents per person: 1 (the crew's own aircraft and its automation; the surrounding traffic shown by the traffic data manager is displayed, not supervised, and is flown by other crews); human measure: NASA-TLX (35.4, 32.5, 33.3), time to first reaction, time to configure, time to first automation update, System Usability Scale; per the 2026-11-14 narrow-clause ruling one aircraft with several automated functions is single-agent; note also that the record is a NASA conference slide deck, so all figures are axis labels on boxplots with no statistics reported, and the mapping of 35.4/32.5/33.3 to dynamic/noisy/static is my reading of the chart labels.

title: Integrating Human-Robot Teaming Dynamics Into Mission Planning Tools for Transparent Tactics in Multi-Robot Human Integrated Teams
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation
evidence: Each participant coordinated FOUR robots; human measures were real-time SAGAT accuracy, NASA-TLX and wedge-formation performance: 'significant difference (W = 103, P = .02, r = 0.53 (large effect)) in situation awareness when participants used Groupthink teaming dynamics versus when they used Individual-Agent teaming dynamics' (Sec. III-B Situation Awareness).
method: Within-subjects pilot study comparing two inter-robot collaboration modalities for supervising a four-robot team: per-robot waypointing (Individual-Agent) versus one group waypoint via the PETAAR/ATAK toolset (Groupthink).
evaluation: Robotics Research Center, USMA; 4 robots per participant; SAGAT 92.78% (Groupthink) vs 87.61% (Individual-Agent), W=103 P=.02 r=0.53; wedge score 12 vs 9.45, W=0 P<.0001 r=0.71; NASA-TLX 2.42 vs 2.68 n.s.; SUS 69.43 vs 68.86 n.s.; duration 4.32 vs 4.05 min n.s.
contribution: Pilot study showing that group-level waypointing through the PETAAR toolset significantly improves operators' real-time situation awareness over per-robot waypointing when supervising a four-robot team.
flag: agents per person: 4. human measure: real-time SAGAT accuracy (92.78% vs 87.61%, P=.02), NASA-TLX, wedge-formation score. Check sample size inconsistency: the text says an a priori power analysis gave 'n = 20 with 10 participants per condition' but also '22 participants' in a within-subjects design, and the Wilcoxon statistics (W=103) fit neither cleanly. Groupthink wedge score of 12 is a ceiling by construction (the robots held formation), so that contrast is not a fair human-performance comparison. Pilot study on a deliberately simple static mission; authors say a harder mission would be needed.

title: Human-assisted navigation through sliding autonomy
venue: 2017 2nd International Conference on Robotics and Automation Engineering (ICRAE)
evidence: Experimental Setup: 'The robot we used is an iRobot Create robot equipped with a Hokuyo laser range finder' - one robot, one operator; Table I reports completion time, solution quality and NASA-TLX per mode.
method: Sliding autonomy interface with four modes (autonomy, semi-autonomy, teleoperation, new peer-to-peer); operator or robot can trigger a mode switch at runtime.
evaluation: Physical search-and-rescue navigation, 3 scenarios x 3 runs, ONE iRobot Create, one operator; completion time 68.6s-122.6s, solution quality 8 of 8 in all modes, NASA-TLX 15-28; no participant pool, no statistics.
contribution: Applies four-mode sliding autonomy, including a peer-to-peer mode, to robot navigation and shows task quality is maintained when the operator takes over from a failing robot.
flag: agents per person: 1; human measure: NASA-TLX (autonomous 15, teleoperation 28, peer-to-peer 26) and completion time (68.6s, 122.6s, 104.6s); title and abstract sell a 'human-robot team' and 'multi-agent team' but the validation is a single iRobot Create with a single operator, so the setting is genuinely single-agent; TLX comes from the authors' own operator, not recruited participants, with 3 runs per scenario and no inferential statistics, so the evaluation floor is also doubtful.

title: Increasing Autonomy Transparency through capability communication in multiple heterogeneous UAV management
venue: IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems
evidence: Each participant supervised FOUR heterogeneous UAVs that requested help by text message; human measures were NASA-TLX, SAGAT and a trust instrument: 'the mean workload experienced in the evaluation experiment (63.53%) is lower than that of the baseline experiment (68.2%)' and mean SAGAT rose from 15.417 to 18.288 of 30, p<0.001 (Sec. VI-A, VI-B).
method: Operators managed four simulated rotary UAVs on a multi-touch tabletop across transit, hazard-avoidance and search modes, with and without text-based messages in which each UAV declared its autonomy and functional capability and asked for help.
evaluation: Within-subjects baseline vs transparent-autonomy conditions, two 10-min missions, N up to 34; NASA-TLX 63.53% vs 68.2% p=0.04; SAGAT 18.288 vs 15.417 of 30 p<0.001; trust competence p=0.033, predictability p=0.045, reliability p=0.025; event response time p=0.001; targets found p<0.001; initial response time p=0.082 n.s.
contribution: Controlled study showing that letting each of four heterogeneous UAVs communicate its autonomy and capability in text lowers operator workload and raises situation awareness, trust and response performance.
flag: agents per person: 4. human measure: NASA-TLX (63.53% vs 68.2%, p=0.04), SAGAT (18.288 vs 15.417 of 30, p<0.001), trust subscales, event response time (p=0.001). Strong fit for (e): the UAVs defer to the operator by requesting assistance at runtime. Sample size varies by measure (N=34 trust, N=32 SA, N=30-33 performance) because outliers were removed; the abstract reports no numbers. Order was counterbalanced only by halves, and baseline always ran first for half the sample.

title: To ask for help or not to ask: A predictive approach to human-in-the-loop motion planning for robot manipulation tasks
venue: 2022 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
evidence: Twenty virtual robots were supervised by one operator, but the warehouse evaluation measured only robot-side quantities: 'Fig. 6-Left shows the average total planning time each robot spent on an RTC problem' and success rate (Sec. VI-C); the 4 participants were used only to collect 1,500 scenes of training data for the human-gain predictor (Sec. VI-B).
method: Predictive Guided Framework learns two cost-gain predictors from robot planner state and assigns the human operator to whichever robot in the fleet would benefit most from high-level guidance, instead of waiting for a planner to get stuck.
evaluation: Virtual warehouse with 1, 10, 20 and 30 robots, PGF vs on-request human-in-the-loop baseline; planning time and success rate (99% ceiling); PGF queried the human at iteration 6 vs 25 on average, and on 307 of 1,000 problems (31%) vs 175 (18%); human predictor RMSE 157.49 vs 58.56 autonomous. No human outcome measured.
contribution: Learned predictors of how much human guidance each robot would gain let a single operator be routed to the neediest robot in a twenty-robot fleet, cutting planning time versus on-request querying.
flag: agents per person: 20 (up to 30). human measure: NONE - the 4 participants only generated training data; all reported outcomes are planning time and robot success rate. Condition (2) is clearly met and the abstract's talk of guiding a fleet promises condition (1), but the full text shows the human in the warehouse runs is a model, so this is the exact abstract-promises-both failure. Worth the maintainer's eye under criterion (a) for another pillar: the mechanism is a genuine runtime deferral gate with a baseline (iteration 6 vs 25), just with no safety metric and no human outcome. Most likely of my ten to be overturned.

title: A VR Study to Explore the Benefits and Risks of eHMI Communication Strategies for Automated Buses
venue: 2025 IEEE 28th International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC)
evidence: Participants were ordinary drivers meeting automated buses, not supervisors of automation: 'In a virtual reality (VR) experiment, 36 participants drove through a simulated residential area under four eHMI conditions' and encountered one bus per unsignalized intersection (Abstract; Sec. II).
method: VR driving study of four external human-machine interface strategies on automated buses (none, status, intention, instruction) at unsignalized intersections with ambiguous right of way.
evaluation: 36 participants, within-subjects, four counterbalanced eHMI conditions, three intersection scenarios, driving behaviour logged at 60 Hz plus subjective trust, comprehension, perceived safety and hesitation ratings; intention and instruction eHMIs reduced hesitation and raised perceived safety.
contribution: VR study showing that intention and instruction external interfaces on automated buses reduce other drivers' hesitation and raise perceived safety, while instruction interfaces risk over-trust.
flag: agents per person: 1 encountered bus at a time, and the participant supervises nothing. human measure: hesitation, perceived safety, comprehension, trust, driving behaviour at 60 Hz. Condition (1) holds, condition (2) fails outright: this is external communication to a surrounding road user, with no supervision, monitoring, teaming or takeover from automation, so criterion (e) does not hold either. If the maintainer counts any encounter with automation as handoff this would still be single-vehicle, hence E4 rather than E1.

title: An Evaluation Framework of Human-Robot Teaming for Navigation Among Movable Obstacles via Virtual Reality-Based Interactions
venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
evidence: Each participant supervised TWO heterogeneous robots (Husky and Jackal): 'Each participant supervised both robots by assigning them goal points and helping them locate the target objects' (Sec. IV-C); completion time fell from 384 s single-user to 228 s multiuser, t(11)=6.99, p<0.01, and NASA-TLX temporal demand fell significantly with autonomous door opening (Sec. IV-B, IV-C).
method: VR framework that fuses a pre-built 3D environment model with live robot sensor data to give operators immersive oversight of a heterogeneous robot team performing navigation among movable obstacles, with optional autonomous NAMO algorithms.
evaluation: Three-phase user study, N=53 total (30 for representation, 12 for single vs multiuser, 12 for algorithms), 2 robots per operator; MP3D+PCS 241 s vs PCS 256 s with 18 vs fewer collisions; 1P_RC 384 s vs MP_RC 228 s, t(11)=6.99 p<0.01; Curriculum RL 311/362 s vs TARE 417/428 s, t(11)=7.86 and 5.13 p<0.01; NASA-TLX temporal demand t(11)=2.73 p<0.05; network latency 25.6 ms (SD 10.7) to 404.5 ms.
contribution: VR oversight framework for heterogeneous robot teams in navigation among movable obstacles, validated in a 53-participant study on operating time, collisions, workload and perceived situation awareness.
flag: agents per person: 2 heterogeneous robots (Husky plus Jackal). human measure: task completion time (384 s vs 228 s, t(11)=6.99, p<0.01), collision counts, NASA-TLX temporal demand (p<0.05), 7-point Likert SA and efficiency items. Borderline on fleet size: two robots is the stated minimum under the ruling, and phase A arguably treats them one at a time. Situation awareness is claimed throughout but only ever measured as Likert agreement items, never with SAGAT or SART; NASA-TLX is reported only as significance on single subscales, with no overall score.

title: Exploring the Impact of Immersion on Situational Awareness and Trust in Remotely Monitored Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships
venue: OCEANS 2023 - Limerick
evidence: Each participant acting as remote control centre operator monitored FIVE autonomous vessels: 'the participant was tasked with monitoring the MASS container ship and its 4 support vessels as they traversed the Davis Strait' (Sec. III), with SPAM-based SA, workload, trust and motion sickness measured; mean SA activation time differed by immersion, F(2,76)=18.86, p<.001 (Sec. IV-A).
method: Simulated remote control centre for a maritime autonomous surface ship escorted by three unmanned surface vehicles and a drone, presented at three immersion levels (non-immersive, semi-immersive and fully immersive VR).
evaluation: 39 participants, within-subjects 3x3 Latin square over three immersion levels; SPAM SA activation time F(2,76)=18.86 p<.001 (IVR slowest), SA percent correct F=0.20 n.s., SA response time F=0.01 n.s., rate-correct score F=0.44 n.s., trust F=1.99 p=.144, motion sickness F=5.17 p=.008, workload F=4.10 p=.020, plus correlations such as workload-trust r=-0.366 to -0.519.
contribution: Study of three VR immersion levels for remotely monitoring an autonomous ship and its four robotic escorts, finding immersion trade-offs between situation awareness, trust, workload and motion sickness.
flag: agents per person: 5 (one autonomous container ship plus 3 USVs and 1 drone, all navigating independently). human measure: SPAM SA activation time (F(2,76)=18.86, p<.001), SA percent correct, trust 1-7, workload, motion sickness (p=.008). Note the headline SA accuracy measures were all non-significant; only activation time, motion sickness and workload reached significance, so the abstract's claimed benefits for semi-immersive VR rest on non-significant means. Participants were mostly a university pool (N=28 of 39), not professional mariners, and the task was monitoring only, with no actual takeover.

title: MOMUx: A Catalyst for Discovering Situational Awareness and Team Coordination Requirements for Human-Autonomy Teaming
venue: 2026 IEEE 34th International Requirements Engineering Conference (RE)
evidence: Teams of three operators supervised a SIX-UAV swarm: 'mission of 18 minutes duration with six UAVs' with asset density raised from three to six (Sec. II-B); SAGAT scores by role and episode gave a 'significant perception (L1) collapse for TO (p = 0.008) and VO (p = 0.007)' at the viewpoint shift and an RPIC comprehension collapse p=0.001 (Sec. III-B).
