contribution: Experimental platform and method that use SAGAT, eye tracking and think-aloud on a shared mission timeline to discover situation-awareness and coordination requirements for multi-operator multi-UAV swarm supervision.
flag: agents per person: 6 UAVs per 3-operator team (3 in the baseline episode). human measure: SAGAT L1-L3 scores with mixed-design ANOVAs (p=0.008, p=0.007, p=0.001), eye tracking, think-aloud. Borderline on paper type: the contribution is a platform and a requirements-discovery method, and the quantitative human results are reported only as p-values, with the role-by-episode SAGAT means shown solely in Fig. 5, so the evaluation floor is met but thinly. Eye-tracking data are described as collected but no eye-tracking figures are reported. Candidate requirements were drafted with GPT-5.2, which the maintainer may want noted.

title: Towards situational awareness from robotic group motion
venue: 2019 28th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN)
evidence: Observers watched five table-top robots on video and rated what the motion conveyed; nothing about the observer's own awareness or performance was scored: 'participants completed a survey comprising two different scales ... seven-point Likert scale' and the analysis reports only Kendall's tau-b correlations between perceived-organisation items and communicative-intent categories (Sec. IV).
method: Two studies building a typology of communicative intents that swarm group motion can convey: free descriptions of five motion sequences by Zooid robots, then an online survey relating perceived group-motion parameters to those intent categories.
evaluation: Study 1: 10 participants describing five motion sequences, 197 verb phrases coded into 7 intent categories. Study 2: 113-participant online survey, 7-point Likert items, Kendall tau-b correlations (largest 0.276 for react-to-each-other with inter-robot communication). No SA score, no workload, no condition contrast, no p-values reported.
contribution: Typology of communicative intents conveyed by swarm group motion, with correlations between perceived motion parameters such as synchronisation and figure formation and the intents observers attribute.
flag: agents per person: 5 table-top robots on video (framed as a proxy for UAV swarms). human measure: NONE that qualifies - only Likert ratings of what the robots' motion signifies, mapped post hoc onto Endsley's SA levels in the discussion. No SAGAT, SART, workload, takeover or error measure, and the only statistics are correlation coefficients with no comparison, baseline or condition contrast, so the evaluation floor fails. Participants are observers, not operators supervising or taking over. The maintainer may be tempted by the swarm-plus-SA framing in the title and abstract; the SA claim is interpretive, not measured.

title: Improving Human Performance Using Mixed Granularity of Control in Multi-Human Multi-Robot Interaction
venue: 29th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication, RO-MAN 2020
evidence: Two operators jointly supervised EIGHT real robots: 'Through a user study involving 28 human operators and 8 real robots' (Abstract), with NASA-TLX, SART, trust scales, activity period and completion time compared across single and mixed granularity of control; interactions differed significantly in the single-granularity condition (Friedman p = 0.0001, chi-square = 14.000) (Sec. IV-C).
method: Augmented-reality mixed-granularity interface letting multiple operators act on a multi-robot system either environment-oriented (moving virtual objects that define goals) or robot-oriented (commanding individual robots, pausing the rest of the team).
evaluation: 28 participants in 14 pairs, 8 real robots, construction task in two phases; single (SGOC) vs mixed (MGOC) granularity; NASA-TLX, SART and trust ranked by Borda count; interactions Friedman p=0.0001 chi-square=14.000 in SGOC vs p=0.109 chi-square=2.571 in MGOC; median completion time 10.63 min (SGOC) vs 7.93 min (MGOC).

flag: agents per person: 8 robots shared by 2 operators (4 each nominally, both able to act on all 8). human measure: NASA-TLX and SART via Borda counts, group and human-robot trust scales, activity period, interaction counts (Friedman p=0.0001), completion time (median 10.63 vs 7.93 min). Weak point for the maintainer: workload, SART and trust are reported only as Borda rank totals per attribute with no inferential test and no effect size, so the only inferentially tested human results are interaction counts and activity period; the completion-time difference is reported as medians with p=0.109 for activity period and no test of time itself.

title: Human-Robot Interaction using VAHR: Virtual Assistant, Human, and Robots in the Loop
venue: 2023 32nd IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN)
evidence: Sec IV: 'The experiment involves one test user controlling two robots'; 10 participants each supervised 2 simulated mobile robots plus pick-and-place arms; human measures were Robot Attention Demand (0.44 vs 0.75), fan-out and NASA-TLX.

evaluation: 10 participants, 2 robots in Gazebo plus a jigsaw secondary task; RAD 0.44 vs 0.75 (p=7.3e-7), fan-out 578s vs 314s (p=6.3e-4), interaction time 111s vs 175s, 13 vs 8 puzzle pieces (p=3e-2); NASA-TLX contrasts all n.s. (combined p=0.28).

title: Human-Autonomy Collaboration for Escaping Local Minima
venue: 2025 34th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN)
evidence: Sec III: 'Participants supervised two UGVs while simultaneously performing a secondary task'; each of 42 participants assisted 2 UGVs at 12 stuck events (6 per UGV); human measures were waypoint decision time (9.48s vs 14.9s) and path deviation.

evaluation: 42 participants, 2 UGVs, 12 local-minima events, spot-report secondary task; path deviation 34.0m vs 102.2m (F(1,29)=12.41, p=.001) and 80.9m vs 179.0m (F(1,36)=4.33, p=.045); decision time 9.48s vs 14.9s (p=.160); secondary task n.s. (p=0.128); 78% preferred cursor.

title: Agent Transparency for Human-Agent Teaming Effectiveness
venue: Proceedings - 2015 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC 2015
evidence: Sec III: IMPACT study has an intelligent agent for 'multi-robot management' with ground, aerial and surface platforms, 30 participants choosing between agent plans; Sec II ASM study has 45 participants monitoring one robot; measures were trust scales, SA probes, NASA-TLX, proper agent use and correct rejection.

evaluation: ASM 45 participants between-subjects, IMPACT 30 participants within-subjects over 3 blocks of 8 missions; L1+2 raised proper agent use by 11% and correct rejection by 12%, uncertainty added 2% and 14% more, reaching 90% proper use and 81% correct rejection; ASM SA probes hit ceiling, NASA-TLX n.s.

flag: agents per person: ASM 1 robot, IMPACT a heterogeneous robot team of ground, air and surface platforms | human measure: Trust in Automated Systems and function-specific trust, SA probes, NASA-TLX, proper use and correct rejection percentages | this is a 4-page summary of two studies published in full elsewhere, so exclude-E3 is defensible; percentages are given with no inferential statistics; it reports the same two projects as doi:10.1109/smc.2016.7844505 in this batch (year 1 vs year 2) so check for double counting; the ASM half is single-agent.

title: Effects of Agent Transparency on human-autonomy teaming effectiveness
venue: 2016 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC 2016 - Conference Proceedings
evidence: Sec III: IMPACT had 53 participants teaming with an intelligent agent managing heterogeneous unmanned vehicle (UxV) teams; Sec II ASM had 60 participants monitoring one ASM robot with SAGAT; measures were SAGAT SA, trust, NASA-TLX and total correct responses.

evaluation: ASM 60 participants: SAGAT Level 3 SA F(3,165)=3.87 p<.05, Level 2 SA F(3,165)=3.98 p<.01, trust F(3,165)=5.87 p<.01, workload n.s.; IMPACT 53 participants: total correct F(2,104)=10.31 p<.001, proper use F(2,104)=10.66 p<.001, trust MANCOVA F(4,202)=2.61 p<.05, NASA-TLX n.s.

title: Trust of Humans in Supervisory Control of Swarm Robots with Varied Levels of Autonomy
venue: Proceedings - 2018 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC 2018
evidence: Sec IV: 'The swarm consisted of 32 homogeneous robots'; 20 participants supervised that swarm under manual, mixed-initiative and autonomous LOAs, with the system able to force a control switch that the operator could reverse; measures were trust surveys, a 30-second in-process trust slider and NASA-TLX.
method: Human-swarm supervisory control study of 32 flocking robots at three levels of autonomy, including a mixed-initiative level that switches control between operator and search algorithm when performance declines.

title: Human-Robots Team Cooperation in Crisis Management Mission
venue: Proceedings - 2018 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, SMC 2018
evidence: Sec IV: each operator sat in a command post and cooperated with two Lego Mindstorms robots over 6 sectors, assigning sectors and adapting levels of automation; 18 participants in WithInfo vs WithoutInfo conditions; measures were NASA-TLX, a recall-drawing SA score and task performance.

flag: agents per person: 2 robots | human measure: NASA-TLX weighted workload, drawing-recall SA score, task performance | weakest evaluation in the batch: the SA contrast is only a trend (p=0.08), global TLX is n.s. (p=0.48), and only two TLX subscales reach p<0.05; no numeric means appear in the text, so exclude-E2 is defensible if the maintainer requires reported figures.

title: Adaptive Mission Planning: Evaluation of a Hybrid Cognitive Mixed-Initiative Planning Assistant in Manned-Unmanned Teaming Operations
venue: 2024 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
evidence: Sec I: 'a single Manned-Unmanned-Teaming (MUM-T) team comprising one manned fighter jet and three Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs)'; 10 German Air Force pilots planned and flew with the agent; measures were NASA-TLX, SART, trust, acceptance and mission success.
method: Planning Assistance Agent using hybrid mixed-initiative planning to adapt MUM-T mission plans in real time, evaluated at medium, high and situation-adapted assistance levels against unassisted pilot planning.
evaluation: 10 experienced pilots (15906 combined flight hours), 1 jet plus 3 UAVs, four static situations and dynamic simulator missions; mission success 8of10 situation-adapted, 7of10 medium (447s mean ingress), 4of10 high; dialog processing 7.83s high vs 10.14s medium vs 14.73s adapted; 32.5% preferred the agent plan vs 67.5% own; NASA-TLX no significant reduction, SART highest with adapted assistance.

title: Development of a Support System for Situation Awareness and Decision of Beginner Navigators Using Voice Information
venue: Conference Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man and Cybernetics
evidence: Sec IV: 14 cadets each conned one own ship in a bridge simulator with one voice advisory system; the surrounding vessels are scripted simulator traffic, not automation the cadet supervises; SAGAT was taken at 4 interruptions and timely VHF action succeeded for 6of7 (85.7%) with support vs 4of7 (57.1%) without.
method: Voice-information support system that raises the lookout priority of a crossing target ship and prompts avoidance action, evaluated with SAGAT in a ship-handling simulator.
evaluation: 14 cadets, 7 with and 7 without voice support; SAGAT measurement papers at 6, 11, 16 and 21 min; appropriate-action success 85.7% vs 57.1%; per-subject VHF times tabulated (7.3 to 27.1 min); three without-support subjects showed delayed SA.

flag: agents per person: 1 (one own ship advised by one voice support system; other ships are scripted traffic, not supervised automation) | human measure: SAGAT priority ratings and time to VHF action, 85.7% vs 57.1% success | criterion (1) is clearly met but the setting is genuinely single-agent, so condition (2) fails and this is E4 rather than E2; the maritime-autonomy framing in the abstract is motivation only; no inferential statistics with 7 per group.

title: An Exploratory Study on Human-Robot Interaction using Semantics-based Situational Awareness
venue: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
evidence: Sec IV: each participant controlled one robot that 'can operate in two different LoAs: teleoperation and autonomous navigation modes' and switched LoA at will in a simulated search-and-rescue arena; 14 of 16 participants analysed; NASA-TLX W=11.0 P=0.007 r=0.724.
method: Semantics-based framework displaying signs of human activity, radiation level and laser-noise indicators to a single-robot operator during a simulated disaster-response mission with level-of-autonomy switching.
evaluation: 16 recruited and 14 analysed, within-subjects with vs without semantic indicators, 5-min trials plus a parallel mirror-image task; Wilcoxon: LoA switch response time P=0.040 r=0.570, NASA-TLX P=0.007 r=0.724, situational trust P=0.031 r=0.577; victims found (P=0.102), trust in system (P=0.080) and all parallel-task metrics n.s.
contribution: Shows high-level environmental semantics lower operator workload, speed level-of-autonomy switching and raise trust in own situation awareness during single-robot disaster response.
flag: agents per person: 1 robot | human measure: NASA-TLX, response time to switch LoA, situational trust scale | the human measures are the strongest of any excluded record here, but the deployment is one robot per operator so condition (2) fails; the abstract's 'Human-Robot Team' and plural 'robots' wording is the misleading cue, and despite the SA framing no SA instrument (SAGAT or SART) is used, only trust in one's own SA.

title: Transparency for a Workload-Adaptive Cognitive Agent in a Manned-Unmanned Teaming Application
venue: IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
evidence: Experimental Evaluation: 'With the aid of three UAVs, the participants had to plan and subsequently perform a helicopter transport mission'; participants approved or declined the agent's planning proposals, with freeze-probe SA recall, SART, trust and Bedford workload.
method: Transparency levels from the SA-based agent transparency model added to a workload-adaptive cognitive agent that manages systems and proposes mission-planning interventions in manned-unmanned teaming.
evaluation: Human-in-the-loop helicopter simulator, 10 participants, within-subjects 2 transparency x 2 automation level x 2 task (planning, system management), 3 UAVs plus own helicopter; SA recall higher with transparency (dav=1.617 p=0.008 planning low-LOA; dav=2.704 p<0.001 system management); response time faster (dav=0.529 p=0.003); accuracy and trust ns; SART ns.
contribution: Shows that implementing SA-based agent transparency in a workload-adaptive cognitive agent raises operator situation awareness and speeds proposal validation in a manned-unmanned teaming mission.
flag: agents per person: 4 vehicles (own helicopter plus 3 UAVs) mediated by one cognitive agent; human measure: freeze-probe SA recall at three SA levels, SART, Trust between People and Automation plus Godspeed, Bedford mental workload, response time and decision accuracy; only 10 participants (students, not aircrew), no control group, and the authors admit the a-priori power analysis was not met, so trust and accuracy effects are non-significant; SART showed no change while the freeze probe did.

title: Demand-Driven Transparency for Monitoring Intelligent Agents
venue: IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
evidence: Sec IV: 'The scenario included 12 different UxVs with a range of 9 different capabilities'; 30 analysed participants (15 demand-driven, 15 sequential) monitored one intelligent planning agent's plans for that fleet; measures were plan-selection accuracy, completion time (p=0.04), error detection and perceived trust.
method: Compares demand-driven transparency, where the operator requests explanation levels as needed, with fixed sequential transparency over an explanation-tree model for an intelligent planning agent.
evaluation: 36 recruited and 30 analysed, 12 tasks with a 4-min limit over 12 UxVs; mission success 5% higher for DDT but n.s. (p=0.62), Plan-A trials 55% vs 41%, completion time 55% vs 65% of the limit (p=0.04), 14.6 vs 9.8 transparency levels visited (t(358)=3.48, p=0.001), injected hard-constraint error caught by 27% vs 0% (t(28)=2.26, p=0.03), perceived trust 4.04 significantly higher; usability n.s.
contribution: Shows letting operators pull agent explanations on demand cuts decision time and raises trust and error detection versus fixed sequential transparency when supervising a 12-vehicle fleet.
flag: agents per person: 12 UxVs planned by one intelligent agent | human measure: plan-selection accuracy, completion time, hard-constraint error detection, perceived trust, usability | closest record in the batch to dual-speed handoff, but the headline accuracy difference is n.s. (p=0.62) and no SA instrument is used despite the SA framing; the significant results are completion time, levels visited, error detection and trust.

title: Investigating HMIs to Foster Communications Between Conventional Vehicles and Autonomous Vehicles at Intersections
venue: IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
evidence: "Each condition featured two variations, with an AV situated at two different intersections" (Sec. III-G Scenario Design in VR); SA was measured at those two single-AV interactions (Sec. IV-A).
method: VR driving simulator study comparing no-interface control, external eHMI and internal iHMI through which an AV communicates right-of-way intent to a conventional-vehicle driver at malfunctioning-light intersections.
evaluation: 44 of 50 participants analysed, within-subjects 3 conditions; SAGAT-style SA F(2,131)=13.64 p=.000 eta2=.132, trust F(2,131)=25.20 eta2=.233, pupil diameter F(2,113)=6.69 p=.002, speed change F(2,119)=10.98.
contribution: VR study showing an in-vehicle AV-intent interface raises conventional-vehicle drivers' situation awareness and trust at intersections more than an external display or no interface.

Human outcomes are strong and the evaluation floor is comfortably met, but the participant manually drives a conventional vehicle and meets one AV at a time; nothing is supervised or taken over, so condition (2) genuinely fails. Also note six participants were dropped for eye-tracking and calibration failures, so n varies by measure (44 for SA, 38 for gaze).

title: Augmenting Human Hazard Situational Awareness With Haptic Interface for Heterogeneous Autonomous Vehicles
venue: IEEE Transactions on Human-Machine Systems
evidence: "In the ground scenario, eight adversarial vehicles surrounded the ego vehicle ... Up to three (random) adversarial vehicles will autonomously accelerate to 15 m/s and drive straightforward toward the centre" (Sec. III Experiment Design); aerial scenario used 14 adversarial drones.
method: Low-cost vibrotactile vest encoding 3-D direction of adversarial hazards for an operator monitoring an autonomous ego ground vehicle or ego drone through four camera views in AirSim.
evaluation: 39 participants (21 Phase 1, 18 Phase 2), visual-only vs visual-haptic vs haptic-only; risk detection rate 0.783 to 0.961 ground and 0.778 to 0.923 aerial (p<0.001), hit rate 0.375 to 0.689, time-to-decision 20.22 s to 12.65 s ground and 20.58 s to 14.88 s aerial.
contribution: Human-subject evidence that a low-cost vibrotactile vest raises hazard detection accuracy and cuts decision time for operators monitoring autonomous ground and aerial vehicles under adversarial attack.
flag: agents per person: 1 autonomous ego vehicle plus 8 autonomous adversarial vehicles (ground) or 14 adversarial drones (aerial) to monitor human measure: risk detection rate, hit rate, false detection rate, time-to-decision (TTD), SART. MOST LIKELY TO BE OVERTURNED in this batch: condition (2) is arguable because the person supervises a single ego vehicle and the other autonomous entities are hazards rather than supervised teammates, so exclude-E4 is defensible; ground and aerial are two separate single-ego scenarios, not one heterogeneous fleet. SART was collected but no SART figures appear in the body. EEG and EMG were recorded but explicitly not analysed.

title: Comparisons of Adaptive Automation Conditions for Single-Operator Multiple-Agent Control Systems
venue: 2018 IEEE International Symposium on Technologies for Homeland Security, HST 2018
evidence: "a single operator is assigned multiple agents to complete various ... agents to navigate to suspicious targets and verify the presence of enemy units ... at least one and up to six agents at a given time" (Sec. III SOMAC).
method: SOMAC simulation of single-operator multiple-agent UAV supervision with four automation-allocation schemes that add or remove active agents based on performance or on an EEG-free workload estimate.
evaluation: 24 participants, 4 conditions (adaptable AA, performance-based PAA, hybrid HAA, weighted-random WRA); active agents F(3,80)=17.371 p<0.001 (HAA M=4.362 vs WRA M=3.324), embedded SA score F(3,196)=9.07 p<0.001, NASA-TLX F(3,92)=3.38 p<0.05.
contribution: Controlled comparison of four automation-allocation schemes for one operator supervising up to six UAV-like agents, showing adaptive schemes sustain more active agents at lower measured workload.
flag: agents per person: 1 to 6 agents, mean active 3.32 to 4.36 human measure: NASA-TLX (F(3,92)=3.38, p<0.05), embedded change-detection SA score (F(3,196)=9.07, p<0.001), mission performance score. Worth checking: overall SOMAC score did NOT differ across conditions, so the performance claim rests on number of active agents, not mission score; and the weighted-random WRA condition gave the highest SA score and lowest workload, which the authors do not reconcile with their hypotheses. Exact TLX means are not printed, only the F test and the direction.

title: Unmanned Ground Vehicle Platooning Under Cyber Attacks: A Human-Robot Interaction Framework
venue: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
evidence: "Twenty students from Clemson University (7 female and 13 male) participated in this experiment" and "if an abnormal UGV is identified, the participant can manually intervene in the longitudinal control of the abnormal UGV via the joystick" (Sec. VI-C).
method: Observer-based resilient platoon controller plus an anomaly reporting system, Bayesian trust-based information management and a decision-aid GUI that lets one operator detect hacked UGVs and seize longitudinal control of them.
evaluation: 9-UGV platoon simulation with 9 camera views, 20 participants, proposed GUI-N vs baseline GUI-B; platoon vulnerability -78.4% (Wilcoxon p<0.001), NASA-TLX workload -39.0% (p<0.001), missed-detection time -44.8% (p<0.001), platoon efficiency unchanged (p=0.167).
contribution: Human-supervised UGV platoon framework whose trust-filtered decision aid lets one operator take over hacked vehicles, cutting measured platoon vulnerability and operator workload against a baseline GUI.
flag: agents per person: 9 UGVs in one platoon, 3 of them hacked human measure: NASA-TLX (-39.0%), missed-detection time (-44.8%), platoon vulnerability (-78.4%), all GUI-N vs GUI-B with n=20. Strongest fit in the batch and the only one with a genuine runtime override by the human. Check: the human-subject set reported here had NO V2C cyber attack injected even though participants were told one might occur, so the human-correction-of-trustworthiness (HCT) algorithm is supported by simulation only, not by people; per-condition TLX means are not printed, only the percentage change.

title: Rapid Prototyping & Evaluation of Crew Stations to Support Manned-Unmanned teaming
venue: Proceedings - 2025 IEEE Conference on Virtual Reality and 3D User Interfaces Abstracts and Workshops, VRW 2025
evidence: "The task required participants to control a robotic vehicle remotely, using a crew station interface to search for and identify target figures within a rescue area" (Sec. 3 Method).
method: Crew-station prototypes for manned-unmanned teaming built at four points of the reality-virtuality continuum (real, AR, augmented virtuality, VR) and compared on operator performance and experience.
evaluation: 4x1 within-subject, 8 participants, real vs AR vs AV vs VR; task completion time, visual search time, error rate, SART SA, presence, SUS, Modified Cooper-Harper workload, preference - every result stated only as "comparable" or "worse", with no value or test statistic.
contribution: Two-page report that AR, augmented virtuality and VR crew-station prototypes reproduce real-world operator performance, situation awareness and workload for remote robotic-vehicle operation.
flag: agents per person: 1 remotely controlled robotic vehicle human measure: SART SA, Modified Cooper-Harper workload, task completion and visual search time, error rate, SUS, presence - but not one numeric value or test statistic appears in this 2-page VRW abstract, so the evaluation floor fails. Condition (2) also fails since each participant drove a single robotic vehicle, so exclude-E4 is equally defensible; the conclusion also credits "haptic or tactile feedback" for the AR and AV results although haptics was never an independent variable in the method.

title: Situation awareness-based agent transparency for human-autonomy teaming effectiveness
venue: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering
evidence: "participants were asked to monitor UxVs patrolling a [region] ... Results suggested that operators were more likely to make correct decisions regarding intervention plans whenever they were presented with SAT 1+2+3+U" (Sec. 2.1 IMPACT).
method: Invited overview of the Situation awareness-based Agent Transparency (SAT) model, illustrated by narrative summaries of two previously published programs: IMPACT multi-UxV management and the Autonomous Squad Member ground robot.
evaluation: No new study. Second-hand recounting of prior IMPACT and ASM human-in-the-loop experiments using SART, unweighted and weighted NASA-TLX, SAGAT-style queries and the Trust in Automation scale; no sample sizes, means, effect sizes or p values anywhere in the body.
contribution: Overview of the three-level situation-awareness-based agent transparency model and of two Army human-autonomy teaming programs that reported better operator performance and trust as transparency rose.
flag: agents per person: multiple UxVs under one intelligent agent in IMPACT, 1 robot in ASM human measure: SAGAT-style SA, SART, NASA-TLX, Trust in Automation - all reported second-hand. Zero figures in the body, so the evaluation floor fails; exclude-E3 as a review is equally defensible. Near-duplicate of doi:10.1145/3029798.3038339 in this same batch, same authors and same two studies. The primary sources the maintainer should chase are Mercado et al. Human Factors 2016 [17], Stowers et al. 2016 [18] and Selkowitz et al. [14].

title: Assessing multi-agent human-autonomy teams: US Army Robotic Wingman gunnery operations
venue: Proceedings of SPIE - The International Society for Optical Engineering
evidence: "Wingman consists of a command and control (C2) vehicle with a human crew and at least one unmanned, robotic asset ... It is paired with an unmanned weaponized robotic ground vehicle" (Sec. 3).
method: Review of candidate performance, stress, trust and communication metrics for human-autonomy teams, plus an exploratory field data collection during US Army Robotic Wingman live gunnery operations.
evaluation: October 2018 gunnery-range field test, two crews of four Warfighters (Marine and Army) across dry-fire, blank-fire and stationary live-fire runs; crew qualification scores per target engagement (Marine live total 327, Army live 563), ITS, NARS, PSS, Empatica E4 EDA and HR; authors state data were too limited for inference.
contribution: Methodological review and exploratory field assessment proposing performance, stress, trust and communication metrics for crews operating a weaponised robotic ground vehicle during live gunnery.
flag: agents per person: 1 robotic ground vehicle paired with a 5-person C2 crew human measure: crew gunnery qualification score (Table 1), trust rating, NARS, PSS, EDA and HR from wearables. The "multi-agent" of the title means one human team plus one robot, not several automated agents, so condition (2) genuinely fails. The paper is also mostly a metrics review and states explicitly that inferential statistics are left to future exercises, so exclude-E2 or exclude-E3 would fit too.

title: Human-autonomy teaming and agent transparency
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction
evidence: "In the IMPACT study, we examined the level of information necessary to create an effective and transparent interface to support human teaming with an intelligent agent (IA) for multi-robot management in a series of simulated military missions" (Sec. 3).
method: Two-page summary of SAT-model-based interfaces for two environments: dismounted infantry with the Autonomous Squad Member robot, and an operator teaming with an intelligent agent that manages heterogeneous ground, aerial and surface robots (IMPACT).
evaluation: ASM human-in-the-loop study with 60 participants over four SAT display conditions, and IMPACT study with 53 participants over three transparency levels; results given only as "greater trust", "most effective at maintaining SA" and "significantly greater" proper use and correct rejection, with no means or p values.
contribution: Short report that raising agent transparency along the three SAT levels improved operator decision quality and trust calibration in both single-robot and multi-robot human-autonomy teaming interfaces.
flag: agents per person: a team of heterogeneous ground, aerial and surface robots under one intelligent agent in IMPACT, 1 robot in ASM human measure: SAGAT-style SA, NASA-TLX workload, Trust in Automation, proper-IA-use and correct-rejection rates. Sample sizes are given (60 and 53) but no numeric result or test statistic at all, so the evaluation floor fails. Near-duplicate of doi:10.1117/12.2263194 in this batch; both are pointers to Selkowitz et al. HFES 2016, Stowers et al. HFES 2016 and Mercado et al. Human Factors 2016, which are the records actually worth screening.

title: Keep me in the loop: Increasing operator situation awareness through a conversational multimodal interface
venue: ICMI 2018 - Proceedings of the 2018 International Conference on Multimodal Interaction
evidence: "Normally a mission involving a single AUV can be a relatively sedate affair taking some time to complete ... we compressed mission time eight fold" (Sec. 4.2 Procedure); the evaluated dialogue concerns one vehicle, "Auv1", with three objectives.
method: MIRIAM, a conversational agent placed beside the SeeTrack command-and-control display so an operator can query autonomous underwater vehicle status, faults and mission progress in natural language and receive pushed alerts.
evaluation: 16 expert AUV engineers, one simulated Neptune mission, observational (no interface control condition); frozen-probe SA 85.2% correct (SD 11.4), chat used more than the map (Mdn 6 vs 4, T=4, p<.01, r=-0.69), partial correlation of SA with chat use controlling for OSIVQ spatial imagery, SUS 75.6, concept accuracy 0.79.
contribution: Evaluation evidence that adding a conversational agent to an autonomous-vehicle command-and-control interface supports operator situation awareness regardless of visual or verbal cognitive style.
flag: agents per person: 1 simulated AUV with 3 objectives, even though the Neptune framework and the motivation are about multiple vehicles human measure: frozen-probe SA 85.2% correct, information-source frequency, SUS 75.6, user satisfaction 3.0 of 5. Condition (2) fails on the study as actually run. The authors also state they deliberately did not frame it as an experiment with conditions, so the only contrast is chat-versus-map within one interface rather than interface-versus-baseline, which makes the evaluation floor shaky as well.

title: Towards enhancement of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operators' situation awareness: How often should their command and control map be updated
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction
evidence: "Nine participants, all professional military UAV operators participated. They were asked to perform a two-phased mission mimicking an urban battlefield scenario" (Sec. 3 Experiment).
method: Wizard-of-Oz emulation of the GiCoMAF machine-learning command-and-control map filter, testing how often the item-level declutter rule should be re-applied for a UAV operator monitoring a payload feed.
evaluation: 9 professional UAV operators, within-subject 20 s vs 40 s filter update rate; enemy detection 39% vs 26%, misidentification 18% vs 36%, detection lag 165 s vs 193 s, SWAT workload 26 vs 33 on a 0-100 scale; no test statistics reported.
contribution: Operator study showing a 20-second refresh of an intelligent command-and-control map filter yields better enemy detection and lower workload than a 40-second refresh for UAV operators.
flag: agents per person: 1 UAV at one operator workstation human measure: adapted SAGAT (39% vs 26% true-positive reports, 165 s vs 193 s lag) and SWAT workload (26 vs 33). The quantitative contrast means the evaluation floor is met, but the operator flies a single UAV and the many items on the C2 map are map symbols and enemy entities, not automated agents, so condition (2) fails. Also a 3-page late-breaking report with n=9 and no inferential statistics; reference [8] is miscited for SAGAT.

title: I need your help... or do I? Maintaining situation awareness through performative autonomy
venue: ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction
evidence: "Participants viewed the robot's traversal of the ISS through a video window, and were tasked with providing assistance when (ostensibly) required" (Sec. 4.1 Task Design) - one Astrobee robot per participant.
method: Performative Autonomy: robot performs a lower level of autonomy than it has, asking YN or WH questions before acting solely to keep the interactant in the loop.
evaluation: Two online Prolific studies (n=263, n=318), 3 performed-autonomy x 3 n-back workload conditions; SA probe accuracy, 1-5 perceived workload, task accuracy and reaction time.
contribution: Shows that a robot asking for advice it does not need raises operator situation awareness without adding workload, but demonstrates it with one robot only.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one simulated Astrobee robot seen through a video feed) human measure: SA probe accuracy, Performed Low 0.62 (SD 0.24) vs Performed High 0.44 (SD 0.26), BF=12016.97, Performed Medium 0.60 BF=772.28; perceived workload unaffected by autonomy (BF=0.04) while the n-back manipulation moved it (2.62 to 3.88, BF=5.6e11); Experiment 2 added accuracy and reaction time. Criterion (e) is squarely met and the figures are strong, but each participant supervised a single robot, so the multi-agent gate fails - a likely overturn candidate since the paper frames itself as remote supervision of NASA agent fleets. Abstract says n=264, body says 263.

title: Predicting Mental Demand of Teammates Using Eye Tracking Metrics: A Machine Learning Approach
venue: Eye Tracking Research and Applications Symposium (ETRA)
evidence: "Each team managed up to 16 UAVs while multitasking between a primary target detection task and three secondary tasks" (Sec. 2 Methods).
method: Four gaze features (saccade velocity, fixation count, fixation duration, pupil diameter) fed to eight machine-learning classifiers to label NASA-TLX mental demand as low or high.
evaluation: Pooled eye-tracking and workload data from four UAV command-and-control team studies (n=254); 10-fold cross-validation, 8 classifiers compared; kNN best at accuracy 0.81, precision 0.90, AUROC 0.78.
contribution: Gaze features classify team mental demand in 16-UAV command-and-control at 81% accuracy, a step toward real-time operator-state monitoring for multi-UAV supervision.
flag: agents per person: up to 16 UAVs per two-person team human measure: NASA-TLX mental demand (median split) predicted from gaze - kNN accuracy 0.81, precision 0.90, recall 0.84, F1 0.87, AUROC 0.78, against seven other classifiers (Random Forest 0.72, SVM 0.71, Logistic Regression 0.38); all gaze features differed significantly between low and high mental demand, all p<.001. Three-page ETRA short paper reanalysing four earlier studies: the human outcome is a predicted label rather than an experimental effect, and no situation-awareness or takeover measure is reported despite the abstract invoking situation awareness. Maintainer may judge it too thin and overturn to E2.

title: Influencing trust for human-automation collaborative scheduling of multiple unmanned vehicles
venue: Human Factors
evidence: "A goal-based architecture was implemented whereby the human operator guides the high-level goals of the team of UVs (as opposed to guiding each individual vehicle)" with operator-exclusive target identification and weapons-release approval (The Experiment).
method: Trust priming (positive, negative, none) before supervising a decentralized heterogeneous unmanned-vehicle team scheduled by a consensus-based bundle automated scheduler with human approval gates.
evaluation: 48 participants in the OPS-USERS multiple-UV simulator, between-subject priming; validated trust questionnaire, 2-minute real-time trust ratings, area coverage, targets found, mouse clicks.
contribution: Priming gamers toward lower initial trust in a multi-vehicle automated scheduler raised area-coverage performance by 10%, showing trust calibration is a lever for fleet supervision.
flag: agents per person: one operator supervising a decentralized heterogeneous (air and ground) UV team through an automated scheduler; the exact vehicle count is never stated in the text. human measure: trust questionnaire plus real-time trust ratings and system performance - positive-primed group 14.9% higher real-time trust (M=5.54 vs 4.82, Z=-2.614, p=.009); among gamers, positive priming gave 35.2% higher real-time trust (M=6.06 vs 4.48, Z=-2.882, p=.002) but 10% lower area coverage (59.6%, SD 9.2 vs 66.0%, SD 8.4). The headline 10% performance effect is only marginally significant (Z=-1.715, p=.086) and rests on a post hoc gamer subgroup of n=10 and n=12; no SA or takeover-time measure is reported.

title: Understanding Is Key: An Analysis of Factors Pertaining to Trust in a Real-World Automation System
venue: Human Factors
evidence: Method: 'ARS is a fully automated signaling control' setting routes for trains across a workstation, and 'Experienced rail operators in four signaling centers were observed for 90 min' with a trust questionnaire; signallers intervene with trackerball or keyboard to override ARS routing.
method: Observational case study: 5-s activity coding of signallers working with Automated Route Setting across eight workstations, related to a 19-item questionnaire on trust dimensions.
evaluation: 24 observations of 90 min in 4 UK signalling centres, 8 workstations, 21 questionnaire respondents (n=19 analysed); monitoring mean 48% of time (16-73%), intervention 9% (1-19%), quiet time 22%; t-tests high vs low intervention groups: overall trust t(11)=2.478 p<.05, understandability t(11)=2.782 p<.05, faith t(10)=2.373 p<.05; no monitoring effect.
contribution: Field observation of rail signallers shows that understanding of, not reliability of, automated route setting distinguishes operators who intervene often from those who leave the automation alone.
flag: agents per person: many trains routed across a workstation by one central ARS automation, which is the air-traffic-controller analogue the maintainer blessed; human measure: observed monitoring/intervention/quiet-time occupancy and a 19-item trust questionnaire with significant low-vs-high intervention group differences; the contrast is observational and post-hoc (groups formed by splitting the observed signallers), n=19 after exclusions, all male, and traffic levels could not be fully controlled across centres; no takeover-time or SA score.

title: Under Pressure: Examining Social Conformity With Computer and Robot Groups
venue: Human Factors
evidence: "Participants were told that the groups would consist of four agents" whose videotaped answers were shown before the participant responded (Method) - an Asch conformity paradigm, not supervision of automation.
method: Asch-style conformity paradigm in which four virtual computer, robot or human agents answer social (emotion judgement) and analytical (dot arithmetic) trials before the participant answers.
evaluation: 90 participants (30 computer, 29 robot, 31 human), 36 trials, 3x2 mixed ANOVA on conformity rate, plus a 28-participant no-influence baseline and an 82-participant capability calibration study.
contribution: Groups of four computer or robot agents exert an Asch-style conformity effect on human answers, strongest on analytical tasks matching the agents' perceived competence.
flag: agents per person: 4 virtual agents (computer, robot or human group) human measure: conformity rate (Computer 35.56%, Robot 40.37%, Human 44.28%; human vs machine contrast t(87)=2.374, p=.0198; computer vs human t(53.86)=-2.999, p=.012; task main effect F(2,129.876)=53.978, p<.001) and accuracy against a no-influence baseline. Both of the maintainer's two conditions arguably hold (people measured, four agents present), but criterion (e) itself fails: there is no supervision, takeover, handoff or situation-awareness element and no automation deferring to the person, so this is off-topic E1 rather than E4. Maintainer should confirm the choice of E1 over E4.

title: Effects of Touch, Voice, and Multimodal Input, and Task Load on Multiple-UAV Monitoring Performance During Simulated Manned-Unmanned Teaming in a Military Helicopter
venue: Human Factors
evidence: "Participants were told that they were responsible for overseeing two helicopters and three UAVs" while classifying UAV photographs, monitoring warnings and answering radio calls (Method, Procedure).
method: Simulated manned-unmanned teaming crew station in which an Air Mission Commander supervises two Black Hawks and three UAVs using touch, voice or multimodal input.
evaluation: 18 participants, within-subject 3 input modality x 2 task load; target-of-opportunity classification, d-prime, warning reaction time, NASA-RTLX, 3D-SART, PSSUQ, spatial-ability and attentional-control covariates.
contribution: For an operator supervising five manned and unmanned platforms, touch and multimodal input beat voice on detection, reaction time, workload and subjective situation awareness.
flag: agents per person: 5 (two simulated helicopters plus three UAVs) human measure: percentage of target-of-opportunity photographs classified (touch 98.00%, voice 87.06%, multimodal 97.07%; modality F(2,34)=29.17, p<.001, eta2p=.63; task load F(1,17)=37.97, p<.001, eta2p=.69; interaction F(2,34)=13.71, p<.001), d-prime (3.94, 3.75, 3.83; F(2,34)=4.04, p=.048), power-pod warning RT (1.91 s touch vs 5.36 s voice vs 2.60 s multimodal), NASA-RTLX and 3D-SART both favouring touch and multimodal at ps<.05. The RTLX and 3D-SART condition means are not printed in the body - only the ps<.05 claim and the covariate correlations (ACS with 3D-SART r=.47, p=.051; ACS with RTLX r=-.48, p=.045) - maintainer should check Supplement A. The five platforms are monitored, not taken over, and no takeover-time measure exists.

title: The Absence of Degree of Automation Trade-Offs in Complex Work Settings
venue: Human Factors
evidence: Licensed nuclear operators "assigned to eight crews of three operators" executed procedures where, at higher degrees of automation, the system "acted automatically on groups of valves" across the plant (Method).
method: Full-scope nuclear power plant simulator experiment manipulating degree of automation of a Computerized Operating Procedure System across four levels to test lumberjack-model trade-offs.
evaluation: 8 crews of 3 licensed operators, 4 DOA levels crossed with scenarios, counterbalanced; IPAQ situation awareness, perceived task complexity workload, OPAS performance, response time, out-of-the-loop and cooperation self-ratings.
contribution: Full-scope nuclear simulator evidence that situation awareness rose with degree of automation, contradicting lumberjack-model predictions of routine-failure trade-offs in complex work.
flag: agents per person: a three-operator crew supervising procedure automation that acts on groups of valves throughout the plant - many loops under one central automation, includable under the 2026-11-14 ruling rather than several independent agents. human measure: IPAQ situation awareness rose linearly with DOA (contradicting the model), while DOA did not affect perceived-task-complexity workload or failure-task performance on either response time or OPAS; measure sensitivity IPAQ F(3,21)=3.74, p=.03, eta2=0.35 and OPAS F(3,21)=3.23, p=.04, eta2=0.32; self-rated out-of-the-loop performance and human-automation cooperation both worsened with DOA and correlated r=.46, p=.00, r2=.21. The DOA main-effect statistics live only in the RIME figure (Figure 6), summarised in prose but not given numerically in the extracted text, so the quantitative condition contrast must be read off that figure - maintainer should verify. The authors concede IPAQ had not previously appeared in the peer-reviewed literature.

title: Trust Mediating Reliability–Reliance Relationship in Supervisory Control of Human–Swarm Interactions
venue: Human Factors
evidence: Method: 'Thirty-two subjects supervised a swarm of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in foraging missions in which the swarm provided recommendations'; 'A swarm of 20 unmanned aerial vehicles'; operators accept or reject each swarm recommendation.
method: Within-subject manipulation of swarm recommendation reliability in a foraging task, with repeated trust questionnaires and multilevel mediation analysis of reliability, trust, reliance rate and response time.
evaluation: 32 subjects, swarm of 20 simulated UAVs, within-subject reliability conditions, 5 x 2-min intervals per scenario; trust on reliability beta=0.39 CI[0.31,0.47]; reliance on reliability beta=0.34 CI[0.24,0.45] and on trust beta=0.17 CI[0.02,0.33]; AIC 612.7 vs 681 baseline p<.001; means trust 6.14, reliance 0.67, response time 1.52s.
contribution: Confirms with multilevel mediation that trust partially mediates the effect of swarm reliability on an operator's rate of relying on swarm recommendations in supervisory control.
flag: agents per person: 20 UAVs in one swarm; human measure: Jian et al. trust scale, reliance rate, correct-acceptance rate and response time, with random-intercept mediation models against a variance-component baseline; the mediation is partial and the trust path is weak (beta=0.17, CI lower bound 0.02); recommendations are advisory, so the human is an approval gate rather than a takeover; strongest and cleanest human evidence in this batch.

title: Human Performance Benefits of The Automation Transparency Design Principle: Validation and Variation
venue: Human Factors
evidence: "Experiment 1 tested 8 crews of two operators" and "Experiment 2 tested six crews of three operators", with transparency implemented for interlocks, controllers, limitations, protections and automatic programs across the plant (Method).
method: Automation transparency manipulated in the human-system interface (transparent vs traditional) for component-level plant automation in Experiments 1-2 and for procedure automation in dedicated agent displays in Experiment 3.
evaluation: Three full-scope nuclear simulator experiments with licensed crews (8 crews of 2; 6 crews of 3; Exp 3 agent displays), within-subject randomized block factorial designs; response time, OPAS, cooperation, trust, workload, SA.
contribution: Transparent automation interfaces sped operator response and raised task performance and cooperation for component-level plant automation, but the benefit failed to replicate for agent-display procedure automation.
flag: agents per person: a 2-3 operator crew supervising plant automation spanning many interlocks, controllers, protections and automatic programs, and in Experiment 3 procedure automation shown in dedicated agent displays - many loops under one central automation, includable under the 2026-11-14 ruling. human measure: Exp 1 response-time Z-score F(1,7)=13.42, p=0.01; OPAS detections F(1,7)=5.61, p=0.05; OPAS operations F(1,7)=3.67, p=0.10; human-automation cooperation F(1,7)=10.94, p=0.01, eta2=0.61; workload F(1,7)=6.90, p=0.03, eta2=0.50; trust F(1,7)=1.22, p=0.31; self-rated SA F(1,7)=0.05, p=0.83 (null). Exp 2 response time F(1,5)=26.83, p=0.00, eta2=0.85; OPAS detections F(1,5)=11.49, p=0.02, eta2=0.70; OPAS operations F(1,5)=9.06, p=0.03; cooperation F(1,5)=21.10, p=0.01, eta2=0.81. Two cautions: the SA measure itself was null in Exp 1, and Experiment 3 - the agent-oriented condition closest to this review's subject - failed to replicate the transparency benefit. Crews, not individuals, are the unit and df are very small (5-7).

title: Effects of Information Modality and Confidence on Trust and Situation Awareness in Human-Robot Teaming
venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
evidence: "During each mission, participants teamed up with a highly autonomous search and rescue robot with the goal of navigating a disaster-struck hotel to locate survivors" (Methods) - one robot per participant.
method: Wizard-of-Oz urban search-and-rescue mission in which a single autonomous robot conveys medical-triage recommendations as text, graphics or both, with or without stated confidence.
evaluation: 66 participants, between-subject 3 information modality x within-subject 2 confidence conditions, two 20-minute missions; Chancey and TPS-HRI trust scales, 3D-SART, decision time, mission performance score.
contribution: Two-page abstract reporting that graphical transparency sped responses and raised performance while stated robot confidence raised trust, in a single-robot search-and-rescue team.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one wizard-of-Oz autonomous search-and-rescue robot) human measure: Chancey et al. trust scale and TPS-HRI, 3D-SART situation awareness, average decision-making time and a composite mission performance score - but NO figures, p values or effect sizes appear anywhere in this two-page HFES proceedings abstract, only the words significantly faster response times and significantly greater performance scores, and a reported null for modality on trust and SA. The record therefore fails both gates: single-agent (E4) and the evaluation floor of at least one quantitative human result (E2). Maintainer may prefer E2; either way the full paper is not available in this text.

title: Impact of Transparency and Explanations on Trust and Situation Awareness in Human–Robot Teams
venue: Journal of Cognitive Engineering and Decision Making
evidence: "participants were expected to work as a team with a virtual robot in a partially collapsed building" and "to assist the robot during specific interactive tasks" (Methods) - one robot teammate per participant.
method: Minecraft urban search-and-rescue mission with a single virtual robot teammate, crossing robot transparency (dynamic map plus status indicators) with robot explanation in four conditions.
evaluation: Four conditions x two missions split-plot ANOVAs with licensed-free student sample (power analysis asked for 48; df imply about 61); bespoke point-based SA score, trust in robot, team trust, NASA-TLX.
contribution: Robot explanations combined with transparency raised situation-awareness scores and team trust and lowered workload against a baseline, in a single-robot search-and-rescue team.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one virtual robot teammate; the Incident Commander and remote mechanic are human roles, not supervised automation) human measure: bespoke point-based SA score with condition main effect F(3,57)=5.75, p=.002 - baseline below transparency-only p=.027, explanation-only p=.001 and full p=.001 - and mission main effect F(1,57)=12.04, p=.001; team trust F(3,57)=3.37, p=.025; NASA-TLX workload F(3,57)=3.54, p=.020 with baseline above transparency-only p=.034 and full p=.003; trust in the robot showed no condition effect F(3,57)=2.05, p=.117 but a mission drop p<.0001. Criterion (e) and the evaluation floor are clearly met, but the setting is a single robot, so E4. The actual sample size is never stated (the text says the sample was increased above the 48 the power analysis required; df imply roughly 61) and the authors concede their SA scoring system is unvalidated.

title: Design and Optimization of Remote Safety Operator Display Interface for Autonomous Vehicles: A Takeover Performance Analysis
venue: SSRN Electronic Journal
evidence: Section 2.2: 'In the risk scenario monitoring phase, the remote safety operator is required to monitor multiple risk scenarios displayed on the terminal, gain a preliminary understanding of the real-time operational status of each at-risk vehicle'; on the takeover command the operator brakes and steers for the risk vehicle, overriding the automation at execution time.
method: Remote-operation-centre takeover study: questionnaire on multi-scenario layout (72 licensed drivers) then fixed-base simulator orthogonal experiment (42 drivers) varying number of displayed risk scenarios (1-6), update interval (10-25 s), scenarios updated per cycle (1-4) and operator category.
evaluation: 42 participants, 328 takeovers: brake RT range 0.75-0.97 s and steering 0.88-1.14 s across scenario counts; ANOVA scenario quantity F=7.74 p<.001 (brake), update interval F=4.77 p=.001; optimum 4 scenarios plus 15 s interval, 0.94 s composite; consecutive takeovers 0.93 s to 0.88 s to 1.06 s by round 10.
contribution: Simulator study of a remote safety operator supervising several autonomous vehicles, quantifying how the number of displayed risk scenarios, update interval and repeated takeovers degrade braking and steering takeover reaction time.
flag: agents per person: 1-6 (vehicles whose risk scenarios the one operator monitors; a control-room setting, so condition 2 holds under the 2026-11-14 ruling) human measure: braking and steering takeover reaction time (0.75-1.14 s) with ANOVA contrasts. Check two things: the lowest factor level is a single scenario, so part of the design is single-vehicle, and the 'scenarios' are paused video replays rather than live vehicles, so the supervision is of recorded feeds. Update-quantity sums of squares print as 0 with blank F in Table 5, which looks like a reporting error. No SA or workload instrument. Unreviewed SSRN preprint with no abstract in the record.

title: Leveraging Human-AI Collaboration in Crowd-Powered Source Search: A Preliminary Study
venue: Journal of Social Computing
evidence: "a virtual robot autonomously searches a source" and, once a local optimum or endless loop is detected, "crowd workers (humans) are responsible to figure out" the problem and may take full control or set a temporary goal (Secs. 1 and 3).
method: Crowd-powered source search: a runtime detector spots local optima or endless loops in the autonomous searcher and generates crowdsourcing tasks so humans take over, reroute or set a temporary goal.
evaluation: 10 participants (4 experts, 6 non-experts), 200 simulated scenarios and 704 tasks in a 20 m x 20 m area, two algorithmic baselines; success rate, steps, human execution time, SUS, NASA-TLX, interviews.
contribution: A runtime detector that hands a stuck autonomous source-search robot to crowd workers lifted success rate from 78.5% to 100%, with non-experts matching experts.
flag: agents per person: 1 (one virtual robot searcher in a 20 m x 20 m simulated area; multi-robot search is named only as a future direction) human measure: human execution time per task (expert aided control 33.58 +/- 27.87 s, non-expert 29.01 +/- 29.51 s, full control 29.59 +/- 25.47 s and 34.40 +/- 30.16 s; no significant effect, p>0.07 for all pairs), SUS (non-experts aided 80.42 vs full control 65.00; experts 86.25 vs 80.63) and NASA-TLX reported per participant; system success rate 100% against Baseline 1 78.5% and Baseline 2 88.0%, with efficiency control-mode effect F=5.01, p=0.0263. This is the clearest genuine runtime deferral to a person in the batch and would be a strong (a)+(e) candidate, but the supervised setting is a single robot, so the multi-agent gate fails - the most likely overturn alongside record 1. SUS and TLX were reported descriptively with no statistical tests (20 responses each).

title: A Systems Engineering Framework for Vision-Language-Enabled UAV Triage and Disaster Response
venue: arXiv cs.RO
evidence: A preliminary study with seven adult participants completed a baseline condition (standard QGroundControl and terminal interfaces) and an AI-assisted condition (Sec. preliminary human-factors evaluation); each supervised a single simulated UAV workflow, with multi-UAV scalability named as future work; mental demand fell 2.29 to 1.43, effort 2.43 to 1.43 and frustration 2.86 to 1.86 on 1-5 scales, trust mean 4.64.
method: Model-based systems engineering framework (SysML use-case and block-definition views) embedding a vision-language model as an ICS-aligned coordination agent between operator, mission-control logic and UAV task execution, with ROS2-Gazebo-PX4 software in the loop.
evaluation: Software-in-the-loop demonstration plus 7-participant questionnaire, baseline vs AI-assisted; self-report workload 2.29 to 1.43 mental demand, trust 4.64, communication clarity 4.50; no statistical tests, no system metrics, no ablations, no hardware or latency.
contribution: Systems-engineering framework placing a vision-language model as a coordination agent inside the human-UAV loop for disaster triage, with a small questionnaire study suggesting lower operator workload than unassisted ground-control tooling.
flag: agents per person: 1 (a single simulated UAV workflow; the 126-UAV figure in the text is from cited work [9], not this study). human measure: 1-5 self-report workload items with a baseline contrast, mental demand 2.29 to 1.43 across 7 participants. Check: exclude-E4 for the single-agent setting, but exclude-E2 is at least as defensible, since this is an MBSE architecture paper whose only results are descriptive self-reports from 7 participants with no statistical tests, no ablation and no system-level metric; the VLM is described as decision support with the operator issuing the final command, and no runtime veto or halt function is specified.

title: Trust, Attention, Situation Awareness, and Workload in Multi-AUV Control: Part 1 – Anomaly Detection and AUV Monitoring
venue: PsyArXiv (OSF Preprints)
evidence: Section 3.2.1: 'The simulator generated 4 x drift errors between data points for each AUV in a 30-minute session' - each of 95 participants monitored four independently updating AUVs on a map, clicking a per-AUV 'recalibrate' button on alert, while doing a secondary image-classification task; trust, SA (SAGAT-style freeze probes) and NASA-TLX were sampled in-task.

evaluation: 95 participants, 5 alert groups: alert response time 10.4-12.5 s across tones (Tone 2 fastest, Tone 3 slower, est. 2.08 s, ER 14.4); fastest 9.33 s for tones under white noise vs 11.82 s silence; trust flat 3.81-4.30 over 9 blocks.

flag: agents per person: 4 (four independently drifting AUVs, each with its own recalibrate control) human measure: trust (1-7 per-AUV and overall), SAGAT-style SA freeze probes, NASA-TLX, recalibration clicks, alert response time. Note the paper itself declines to analyse the TLX and SA-score results in depth ('we will not investigate these measures directly in this study', s3.2.1) and several result sections present only boxplot figures, so the strongest quantitative contrasts are response-time models; SA effect is reported as null. Part 1 of two studies, so Part 2 may be a companion record. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

title: Strategy development pilot study of sleep-restricted operators using small satellites with displays
venue: Aerospace Medicine and Human Performance
evidence: "The task scenario required that subjects control both SPHERES simultaneously (using the keyboard) in order to avoid collisions between SPHERES or with debris" (Methods, Procedure); SA aid effect measured as Average Directions Correct, which "could take on the value 0, 1, or 2" because each operator tracked two satellites (Statistical Analysis).

Figures: survival time second session mean 55.9 s/median 44.0 s for SS-SR order versus 42.7 s/33.5 s for SR-SS (95% CI -0.014,-0.002 s-1, P=0.002); area covered 0.606 versus 0.289 m2, P<0.0001; Augmentation benefit on Average Directions Correct only for SS-first subjects, chi2(2)=8.012, P=0.018. venue: Applied Sciences (Switzerland)

title: Effects of Robot Speed, Number, and Orientation on Operator Stress and Mental Workload in Human–Robot Collaboration: A Multimodal Assessment Using Physiological and Subjective Measures
venue: Multimodal Technologies and Interaction
evidence: "Two robots increased stress, mental workload, attention, and excitement relative to one robot, with consistent elevations in electrodermal activity, shorter inter-beat intervals" (Abstract); robot number was manipulated as "one or two" cobots working with the operator (Section 2, Experiment Design).
method: Mixed-factor 3x2x2 within-subjects human-robot collaboration experiment varying cobot speed, cobot number (one versus two) and left-right spatial orientation during a Lego stacking task.
evaluation: 30 participants, 8 sessions each; Empatica E4 electrodermal activity, inter-beat interval, skin temperature with linear mixed models, plus NASA-TLX-derived subjective workload, stress, attention and predictability; one-robot condition is the contrast.
contribution: Multimodal evidence that adding a second collaborative robot raises operator stress and workload as much as raising robot speed does, and that two slow robots match one fast robot on subjective workload.
flag: agents per person: 1 versus 2 collaborative robots (the multi-agent condition is two cobots). human measure: subjective total workload, stress, attention, excitement, robot predictability, plus EDA/IBI/skin-temperature physiology. Figures: total workload 11.0 (SD 7.10) with one robot versus 23.0 (16.9) with two, Wilcoxon p=0.001; effort p<0.001; trust-adjacent predictability rated lower for two robots p=0.041; EDA tonic mean 1.04 (1.60) versus 1.25 (1.84), beta=0.015, p=0.048; EDA sympathetic N 0.0064 versus 0.0110, p=0.0044. title: Comprehensive architecture for intelligent adaptive interface in the field of single-human multiple-robot interaction
venue: ETRI Journal
evidence: Simulation and Result: 'To evaluate the IAI, different simulated scenarios were performed by eleven contributors. Each contributor completed operations in two modes: IAI on; IAI off', controlling 3 or 5 UAVs with intelligent collision warnings.

contribution: An ontology-driven adaptive interface for single-human multi-UAV control that lowers operator workload and raises measured and perceived situation awareness against a classic interface.

title: To Shoot or Not to Shoot? Human, Robot, and Automated Voice Directive Compliance With Target Acquisition and Engagement
venue: Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics International
evidence: "Participants were tasked to take commands from a human, NAO robot, and a computer automated voice while deciding on whether to fire upon armed robots, a swarm of drones, or a single drone ... Participants were instructed that the commands given to them might not be correct and it was upon their judgment" (Abstract, Methods).
method: Mixed-measures pilot in which each participant receives fire directives from three sources (human, NAO robot, automated computer voice), with male or female voice between subjects, and must judge whether to engage each target.
evaluation: 14 participants (5 students, 5 ROTC, 4 soldiers), 54 iterations, 20-s response window; target acquisition and engagement accuracy, NASA-TLX, 3D-SART SA; three one-way repeated-measures ANOVAs across directive sources.
contribution: Pilot showing that a soldier's workload, situation awareness and engagement accuracy depend on which automated teammate issues the fire directive, with robot directives lowest in workload but not in awareness.
flag: agents per person: 3 directive-giving entities, of which 2 are automated (NAO robot and automated computer voice); targets included a drone swarm. human measure: NASA-TLX workload, 3D-SART situation awareness, target acquisition and engagement accuracy. Figures: acquisition 98-100% and engagement 93-97% across directive sources; TLX overall 20-27 across sources (human highest, computer lowest), frustration 12 human versus 18 computer versus 13 robot; SA differed between human and robot directives F(2,26)=3.48, p<0.046, partial eta2=0.211; human versus computer SA M=15.64 (SD 4.43), t(13)=13.21, p<0.001, mean SA decrease 2.22; engagement accuracy differed by experience group F(2,22)=3.83, p<0.037, partial eta2=0.258. runtime_interceptor marked yes only because the HUMAN vetoes an automated fire directive at execution time, not because the paper contributes a mechanism. Maintainer should check: N=14 pilot with unbalanced subgroups; the NAO robot was reported faulty and the computer voice "38% ineffective", which contaminates the directive-source contrast; most figures are read off bar charts rather than tabulated; "multi-agent" here means several directive-giving agents, not a supervised fleet.

title: The Impacts of Multi-Agent Quantity, Type and Transparency on Mental Workload, Situation Awareness and Human Out-of-the-Loop
venue: Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics International
evidence: "The condition of quantity 2 means that the human monitors two agents at the same time" (Section, Experiment 1 design); "the more the quantity of agents, the higher the cognitive mental workload, the lower the SA, and the more serious the OOTL degree" (Abstract).
method: Two within-subjects experiments on operators monitoring one versus two autonomous agents (an unmanned-vehicle assignment assistant and a semi-autonomous vessel dynamic-positioning system), then varying agent type and transparency.
evaluation: Experiment 1: 12 participants, 2 (agent quantity) x 2 (agent type); Experiment 2: 22 participants, agent type x transparency; measures NASA-TLX, SART, out-of-the-loop questionnaire and task performance, ANOVA with quantity 1 as contrast.
contribution: Quantifies the cost of adding a second autonomous agent to an operator's span - higher workload, lower situation awareness, deeper out-of-the-loop state - and shows transparency partly offsets it.
flag: agents per person: 1 versus 2 autonomous agents (heterogeneous or homogeneous), total task count held constant. human measure: NASA-TLX, SART situation awareness, out-of-the-loop degree, task performance. Figures: NASA-TLX 39.79 (quantity 1) versus 48.33 (quantity 2), F(1,11)=51.58, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.824; agent type F(1,11)=6.20, p=0.03; SART 24.96 versus 16.63, F(1,11)=18.31, p=0.001, partial eta2=0.625, with quantity x type interaction F(1,11)=5.64, p=0.037 (homogeneous 15.08 heterogeneous contrast t(11)=2.564, p=0.026); OOTL 12.67 versus 15.92, F(1,11)=34.22, p<0.001, partial eta2=0.757. Maintainer should check: cleanest fit to the ruling in this batch - the quantity manipulation IS the multi-agent variable; small N (12 and 22) and a 5-page conference paper, and the Experiment 2 ANOVA tables are reported without the per-cell means in the extracted text.

title: What About the Next Generation? Assessing Experts’ Judgments of Human Abilities Required for Working in a Future ATC Environment
venue: Applied Human Factors and Ergonomics International
evidence: "A controller-in-the-loop simulation study was designed to assess experts' judgments on the main human abilities required for working in time-based arrival scenarios with different levels of assistance by an arrival-management system" (Abstract); in the most automated scenario "the ATCO will have the role of the supervisor of automation ... with the possibility to intervene if required" (Introduction).
method: Controller-in-the-loop simulation of a Frankfurt arrival sector with the AMAN arrival manager as central automation, comparing one manual baseline against four future roles from delegating to monitoring.
evaluation: 5 licensed controllers, 5 runs with 24-plus arrival flights each; eye-tracked gaze transitions between aircraft, ISA and SASHA-type situation awareness, NASA-TLX, AIM and modified F-JAS ability ratings; baseline run is the contrast.
contribution: Shows that delegating trajectory management to an arrival manager did not unload controllers: workload rose, situation awareness fell and gaze transitions showed they could not build attention-guiding expectations.
flag: agents per person: 24-plus aircraft per controller under one central arrival-management system (AMAN), which the maintainer's 2026-11-14 ruling explicitly counts. human measure: NASA-TLX, ISA workload and situation-awareness probes, SASHA-type SA questionnaire, gaze transitions between aircraft, F-JAS ability judgments. Figures: SA significantly lower than baseline in run 3 "ATCO Controls - AMAN Proposes" F(1,4)=9.732, p<0.05, partial eta2=0.709 and run 4 "AMAN Controls - ATCO Monitors" F(1,4)=24.500, p<0.05, partial eta2=0.806 (omnibus F(4,16)=4.063, p<0.05); NASA-TLX only marginal across runs F(4,16)=2.694, p<0.10 but run 5 higher than baseline F(1,4)=9.476, p<0.05, partial eta2=0.703; ISA workload higher in run 2 F(1,4)=64.000, p<0.05, partial eta2=0.970; gaze Z=-2.023, p<0.05 for the AMAN-in-control condition. Maintainer should check: N=5 controllers and the F-JAS part is an expert JUDGMENT survey rather than a performance measure - the inclusion rests on the ISA/SA/TLX/gaze contrasts against the baseline run, not on the ability ratings; the paper is an AHFE conference paper and reports eta2 values with comma decimal separators.

title: BEYOND NAVIGATIONAL SITUATION AWARENESS: DEVELOPING AND EVALUATING SITUATION AWARENESS SUPPORT SYSTEM FOR REMOTE ENGINE ROOM MONITORING AT THE FUTURE SHORE CONTROL CENTRE
venue: Transactions of the Royal Institution of Naval Architects Part A: International Journal of Maritime Engineering
evidence: Abstract and Discussion: 'The overall fault detection rates across all trials remained at thirty-six per cent, albeit a single ship was monitored'; 24 marine engineers, two interface types, SAGAT and 3D SART (Method, Result).
method: Between-subjects comparison of a traditional engine-room interface (type B) against a cognitive-support interface organising information for comprehension (type A) for remote engine-room monitoring at a shore control centre.
evaluation: 24 marine engineers (12 per group), three 8.5-min scenarios of rising difficulty, one simulated ship; SAGAT per-query chi-square e.g. P4 X2(1,N=24)=10.67 p<.01, P5 6.75 p<.01, C1 4.8 p<.05; 3D SART higher for type A (ns); overall fault detection 36%.
contribution: Shows that organising engine-room information for comprehension improves marine engineers' situation awareness and fault detection during demanding remote monitoring, but not during easy monitoring.
flag: agents per person: 1 ship's engine room; human measure: SAGAT query correctness (significant per-query chi-squares), 3D SART and fault detection rate (36% overall); THIS IS MY MOST LIKELY OVERTURN - the engine room contains several separately automated plant loops (diesel generators with uneven loading, HFO purifier, main engine air cooler, boiler) monitored from a shore control centre, which reads like the maintainer's blessed 'plant crew supervising many loops of one plant automation', but the 2026-11-14 narrow-clause ruling puts one vessel with several subsystems alongside the single spacecraft habitat, and the paper itself stresses 'a single ship was monitored', so I have taken E4; the human evidence is otherwise strong and would support include if the clause is read the other way.

title: HUMAN-CENTERED INTERFACES IN INDUSTRIAL CONTROL SYSTEMS: A REVIEW OF USABILITY AND VISUAL FEEDBACK MECHANISMS
evidence: METHOD: sample is "control-room operators, supervisors, and field personnel who have interacted with HMIs during routine and abnormal operations" in SCADA/DCS/PLC plants, so each supervises many separately controlled plant loops and alarms (count per operator not stated); FINDINGS report Likert situation awareness M=3.73 SD=0.67, workload M=2.74 SD=0.71 and self-reported performance M=3.88 SD=0.58.

evaluation: 188 operators, 4 sectors; regression with site-clustered SE: usability beta=.27 p<.001, visual feedback beta=.21 p=.002, R2=.34; SA mediation a1b1=.12 CI[.07,.18]; usability x feedback beta=.11 p=.011.

Most likely of my three to be overturned.

title: Training Human-Robot Teams by Improving Transparency Through a Virtual Spectator Interface
venue: arXiv cs.HC
evidence: "The primary task was to supervise the two UGVs" (Sec. IV-A) and at hazard level 3 "The human subject must help by taking over the UGV" (Sec. IV-A-1).
method: Virtual Spectator Interface replays a simulated two-UGV supervision mission for after-action training review; compared against screen-recording review and verbal-only review in a between-subjects experiment.
evaluation: 66 participants, 1x3 between-subjects; modified SAGAT (max 30) and a performance score; performance 8.7 to 10.4 (p<.001), SA 22 to 24 (p=.05); no condition effect (p=.37, p=.64).
contribution: A virtual spectator interface for after-action review of human-robot teams; it did not significantly raise team performance or situation awareness over screen-recording or verbal review in a 66-subject study.
flag: agents per person: 2 UGVs; human measure: modified SAGAT situation awareness (22+-6.1 to 24+-5.2, p=.05, called borderline) and a performance score combining takeover completion time with object-flagging accuracy (8.7+-1.3 to 10.4+-1.5, T(130)=-6.41, p<.001). Check that a null result satisfies the maintainer: the three review conditions did not differ (change in performance F(2,63)=1.01, p=.37, eta2p=.03; change in SA F(2,63)=.45, p=.64), and the only suggestive effect is in the low-initial-SA subgroup (n=28, F(2,25)=2.56, p=.10, Tukey VSI vs screen recording p=.08). The VSI is a post-mission review tool, so runtime_interceptor yes refers to the in-task takeover at stop signs and the unflagging of wrong robot detections, not to the VSI. record_id is a DOI; the arXiv id 2503.09849 title matches the record title.

title: Haptic Shape-Based Management of Robot Teams in Cordon and Patrol
venue: 2017 12th ACM/IEEE International Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI
evidence: "Results from a user study suggest that haptic feedback significantly improves operator performance in a reconnaissance task when task demand is higher, but may slightly increase operator workload" (Abstract); "The objective of the present work is to investigate the effects ... on operator performance, situation awareness (SA), and workload while managing a small team of robots" (Section 2).
method: Haptic shape-based interface treats an autonomous robot team as a moldable volume: the operator deforms team shape and spacing and feels force feedback, with the team autonomously surrounding and travelling to buildings.
evaluation: Simulated cordon-and-patrol with a dual-monitor workstation and Novint Falcon; 19 participants, full two-factorial haptics x world difficulty, mixed-model ANOVA on percent hotspots found, SA accuracy and response time, NASA-TLX; plus a 7-person no-vision mini-study.
contribution: Haptic shape and spacing control of an autonomous robot team improves an operator's reconnaissance performance under high task demand without degrading situation awareness, supporting heads-up team supervision.
flag: agents per person: one team of autonomous robots per operator (the paper only says "a team of M robots" and never states the team size numerically; figures show roughly 6-8 nodes). human measure: percent hotspots found, SA accuracy and SA response time, NASA-TLX workload, secondary-task reaction time, preference rating. Figures: haptics x difficulty interaction on percent hotspots found F(1,18)=4.94, p=0.039, with haptics significantly better in the hard world (easy-world difference not significant, NE-YE mean -4.805); NASA-TLX interaction F(1,18)=5.19, p=0.035, workload up 1.7% with haptics, no-haptics versus haptics in hard world NH-YH mean -4.757 not significant; SA accuracy affected by world difficulty but not by haptics (trend N-Y mean -2.501, not significant); preference 3.7 of 5. Maintainer should check: THE ROBOT TEAM SIZE IS NEVER STATED, so "more than one agent" is inferred from the team formalism and figures; the interface is the contribution and the human study is supporting, and the SA result is null; detailed statistics are deferred to reference [18], a thesis.

title: Human-in-the-loop planning and monitoring of swarm search and service missions
venue: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems, AAMAS
evidence: "A user study with 24 participants (10 female) was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of the Hybrid Model as a planning and monitoring aid for SSS missions" (Section 2.1); participants chose a swarm size and then had to "determine whether the mission was running normally" among three anomaly types (Section 2.1).
method: Markov-chain Hybrid Model predicts swarm coverage and job-arrival dynamics and is offered to operators as a planning and monitoring aid for swarm search-and-service missions.
evaluation: Between-groups user study, 24 participants, 5 trials each, experimental (Hybrid Model) versus control; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA on swarm size, cost, input time, anomaly-decision time and correct decisions.

Maintainer should check: THIS IS A 3-PAGE AAMAS EXTENDED ABSTRACT - the swarm size and cost results are stated as significant but the means, F values and degrees of freedom are shown only in Figure 2, so the strongest planning claim has no reportable numbers; control-group aid is not described; if the maintainer treats extended abstracts as insufficiently reported this becomes exclude-E2.
